Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays exceeding 4 EeV, utilizing a 7.5 km^2 cleaning surface within the Pierre Auger Observatory, has allowed us to reap a vast harvest of 83 clean events featuring extensive air showers with clear signals detected by both the underground water Cherenkov detectors and the ground-level radio detectors. By combining the precise energy estimates derived from the water Cherenkov detectors and the evenly spread radio signals detected by the ground detectors, we significantly enhanced the accuracy of our energy measurements, down to a 5% margin for the lowest-energy events in this sample. Our study of these highly energetic events, spanning an enormous 12,300 km^2 detection area, revealed a sharp increase in fluctuations from the expected cosmic ray pattern, surpassing predicted levels by 2σ for the most extreme events. One potential explanation for this observation is the presence of massive cosmic particles undergoing interaction with ultralight field particles, instead of the commonly hypothesized origin in active galactic nuclei. Our current understanding suggests that the primary cosmic particles in this range may not be governed by a single, unified component, although further research is necessary to validate this finding and explore the possible effects of particle mass on interaction depth and energy measurements. Our findings also highlight the value of simultaneous multi-observable analyses in exit studies and the importance of incorporating variables related to particle mass and interaction depth in cosmic ray research. Lastly, we outline a tailored strategy for discovering the sources of extremely energetic cosmic rays based on this research, involving simultaneous observations of ground-level radio signals and cosmic messengers, which could be implemented using existing facilities and upcoming experiments. Our analysis of extremely energetic cosmic rays exceeding 4 EeeV, combined with future research, has the potential to greatly advance our understanding of high-energy physics and the cosmos. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that combines external and internal attributes to predict manipulable points and surfaces on objects. We define NDFs in a way that their values remain unchanged under 3D rotations, translations, and reflections, making them agnostic to specific pose configurations. We employ a simple yet effective approach to ensure that our NDFs are SE(3)-invariant by using the output of a max pooling layer applied to the output of our descriptor network as their value. We use NDFs to train an agent that learns a grasp policy for a novel object through pure exploration, without the need for supervision or a separate learning process. Our results show that NDFs effectively accelerate learning and generalize to new poses and orientations for objects that have been previously explored. We also achieve a success rate of over 90% for objects that have narrow contact areas and are difficult to grasp. Our code is available at https://github.com/vishalranjan/ndf.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct tasks: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We integrated the two processes using a proposed resolution framework that combines projection grids and correspondence constraints derived from CNN output. Projections falling within formatted areas on the projection grid are considered valid for constructing correspondence constraints with the object. We further introduced a score named Correspondence Constraint Score (CCS) that assesses the quality of constraints generated from any given view. High-quality constraints are then used to train a robust neural network, DeepHMap++, which achieves superior performance in comparison to baseline two-stage pipelines. Experimental results validate the superiority of our proposed approach. The code is available online at: https://github.com/lingyu-95/DeepHMap++.oral.

This study investigates how spheres interact with running water by being flushed with water, a phenomenon described as liquid entry surface seal. This research, conducted using high-speed cameras, explores various water flow rates and surface roughness in spheres to understand how these factors influence water pressure and friction with the spheres. It was discovered that a specific, consistent pressure is created when water enters the surface of the spheres, a phenomenon unaffected by the speed of the water or surface roughness. Furthermore, reducing surface roughness was found to decrease the level at which water begins to enter the spheres, but has a limited impact. In addition, pressing the spheres together was found to increase this initial entry point. A mathematical model was developed to describe this interaction and its relationship with water flow and surface roughness. It was discovered that this interaction can be both sticky and slippery, depending on the speed of the water and the smoothness of the spheres, and that it is similar to the mathematics underlying the stick-slip phenomenon. We also provide a comprehensive overview of the key components of this formalism, including the complex scalar, vector, and bivector, as well as the complex Weyl tensor and the Ricci tensor and scalar in the curvature matrix formulation. We introduce a technique to create polynomial functions from linear regressions, using a novel approach to determine the coefficients of these polynomials. This method, which employs an integer optimization problem to converge towards the desired coefficients, enables the derivation of polynomial models, including nonlinear features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in a range of applications, including but not limited to regression tasks with multiple features, robust regression, and learning from datasets with outliers. Additionally, we find that it simplifies linear learning models, such as logistic regression and linear neural networks, and enables the inclusion of non-linear features in these models. Compared to alternative methods, our technique outperforms them in various evaluation metrics, as evident from the results presented in the paper. We believe this technique can be a valuable tool for data scientists working with machine learning models and want to make this method openly available for further development and modification. The code is attached to the paper. We also discuss two different ways in which this technique can be incorporated into existing deep learning models. The paper in question was previously known under the title "Deriving Polynomials from Linear Regressions and Integer Optimization".

Code-mixed language refers to text that combines two or more languages, a common practice especially among multilingual people who communicate across cultural boundaries, as seen in social media. As a result, research in NLP within spoken languages like Hindi, Spanish, Malayalam, Panjabi, Marathi, Telugu, Gujrati, Kannada, and many more has led to code-mixed language research. Code-mixed data poses significant challenges, including determining the language of origin, establishing standards for preprocessing, identifying linguistic rules, as well as developing effective models to achieve high performance on classification and machine translation tasks. Notably, research on code-mixed languages has not been well-documented, and existing knowledge about NLP models can rarely be applied directly. Additionally, due to the lack of large datasets available for training and testing, researchers rely heavily on classification tasks, but more research is needed on other tasks like summarization and machine translation. Furthermore, developing code-mixed language models remains a crucial priority, given the vast potential for artificial intelligence in areas like healthcare and beyond, where understanding multiple languages could lead to greater compassion and more accurate diagnoses. In the long run, code-mixed models have the potential to communicate across different languages, enabling machines to interpret the intentions behind actions like clicking buttons, which could significantly advance various applications in fields like healthcare and finance. In conclusion, code-mixed NLP offers immense opportunities, but overcoming the existing challenges requires a combined effort from researchers, healthcare professionals, technology industry leaders, and the general public, given the widespread presence of code-mixed languages online, as seen in platforms like Twitter. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. To further understand and identify potential applications for these materials, we focused on studying the fundamental Ta$_2$O$_5$ state through simulations and theoretical analysis. Using the Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) and the Hybrid Functional HSE06 method, we performed first-principles calculations to determine the material's electronic and geometric characteristics. However, these calculations yielded two possible crystal structure configurations with equivalent energies, making it challenging to distinguish between them. To resolve this difficulty, we employed Monte Carlo simulations of our GGA results, first increasing temperature to investigate the high-temperature phase and then applying strain to the material. These simulations helped us determine the relevant parameters for calculating the free energies of the two configurations and thereby determined the most likely low-temperature Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure as a mixed phase of Anderson and B-Ta$_2$O$_5$ types. To confirm our findings, we compared our results with experimental data obtained through X-ray scattering. The most frequent Ta$_2$O$_5$ state in simulations matches the Anderson phase, which is characterized by ordered layers of tantalum and oxygen atoms. Reddit's 'Big Geographic Sort' refers to the phenomenon where users from different geographic areas tend to congregate with others from the same region, sharing similar cultural affiliations, and distance from urban areas. This research explores the relationship between the 'Big Geographic Sort' and the spread of misinformation on Reddit. By analyzing news posts and comments across the site, researchers found that user affinity for a particular region does not significantly impact the likelihood of them sharing false information. However, it was discovered that misinformation is more likely to disseminate quickly within urban areas, whereas rural areas are more susceptible to widespread adoption of false information. Furthermore, the research reveals that user familiarity with a region can facilitate the acceptance of new, unverified information, which is consistent with theories of trust and uncertainty. The study's findings suggest that strategies to prevent the dissemination of misinformation should focus on platform-level factors, rather than geographic-based interventions. The study also highlights the significance of considering the 'Big Geographic Sort' in analyzing the transmission of misinformation, which is a novel contribution to the field. The research utilizes a large-scale dataset of news posts and comments from Reddit, coupled with regional cultural and demographic information, to achieve these findings. The study's findings have implications for the study of misinformation, as well as the 'Big Geographic Sort', which can be understood through the lens of misinformation transmission. The research in question has been conducted in partnership with the Fact-Checking Center at the Duke Reporters' Lab. The study's findings have been validated by independent analysis using a separate dataset of Twitter users, which has provided additional insights into the role of urban vs. rural areas in facilitating the adoption of false information, as well as the impact of user familiarity with a region on the willingness to engage with new information on Twitter. Humans naturally generate rich auditory feedback while interacting with their environment, which significantly enhances the understanding of their intentions and actions.  Despite the prevalence of auditory feedback during human activity, developing robotic systems that can efficiently comprehend and interpret this feedback remains a challenge.  This issue is particularly pronounced in scenarios where robots are instructed verbally by humans.  To address this problem, researchers typically rely on auditory cues that are deliberately designed and implemented by instructors, which, although effective, requires additional time and technical expertise.  This article presents an investigation into auditory feedback that arises spontaneously as humans perform manipulation tasks in front of robots.  An experiment was conducted in which participants carried out a variety of manipulation tasks with different objects, including real objects and simulated ones, in front of a robot that was observing their actions.  The objective of this research was to examine the types of auditory feedback generated by these participants and to develop a method for automatically analyzing this feedback.  The results of the experiment were used to demonstrate how the simplicity of the robot's learning system, based on sensory observations, can be assessed by analyzing the auditory feedback that it receives.  The findings of this research can be used in various applications where robotic systems are instructed by humans, including factories, homes, and educational settings.  In these environments, robots can be designed to easily understand the auditory feedback generated by human instructors with minimal setup required.  This research also raises important questions about the inevitability of human activity producing sound and the automatic generation of audible signals from simulation environments.  This article includes an appendix that contains a manually annotated dataset of auditory feedback from one of the manipulation tasks used in the experiment.  This annotation provides an in-depth explanation of the relevant auditory feedback and can be used as a starting point for the automatic analysis of similar feedback in other scenarios.  This research can be extended further by investigating the issues related to sound production that are inherent to certain manipulation tasks and the development of more sophisticated methods of annotating auditory feedback based on textual descriptions of tasks and environments.  This article is the expanded version of the paper that was previously presented at Human-Centric Robotics in 2021.  This expanded version includes an additional section that discusses the challenges related to the production of sound during human activity and the annotation of auditory feedback, as well as two new appendices that contain the detailed analysis of the dataset used in the experiment and the discussion of the issues related to the presence of background noise in the dataset.  This version also includes the corrections for the equations and theorems listed in the paper.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target scenarios are common paradigms used in cross-domain recommendation. In the single-target setting, recommendations are made for one user with multiple preferences, while in the dual-target setting, recommendations are made for both a user and an item with multiple preferences. Due to the pervasive data sparsity issue, the item domain is often more sparse than the user domain. Therefore, we propose a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation, which involves making recommendations for both users and items with multiple preferences in two separate domains, one being more sparse than the other. Since item domain is often more sparse than the user domain, real-world data is used to adjust the framework for typical scenarios. The framework is then expressed as an iterative process to increase efficiency. To deal with the complexity of the model, deep learning is used to convert the model into a dementia-like state known as sparse domain dementia. This state is further leveraged to explore the possibility of transferring knowledge from the dense domain to the sparse domain. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the model's performance is evaluated on multiple public datasets in the single-target and dual-target settings, as well as real-world datasets in the multi-sparse-domain setting. However, there is a lack of dedicated tools that can resolve natural conic expressions to yield pure conic expressions. To address this gap, this work introduces Hypatia, a dedicated package for converting natural conic expressions into their pure form. We demonstrate the benefits of using natural conic expressions through applications in modeling, including an analytical example and the solution to a real-world industry problem involving significant integer constraints. The code for these examples is provided within the package repository available on GitHub. Although Hypatia is specifically designed to be used in conjunction with JuMP, its capabilities can be accessed by other modeling languages due to its utilization of mathematical programming interface standards. The package is named Hypatia in honor of the ancient Egyptian priestess who facilitated mathematical and scientific understanding, and it is intended to assist users in mastering the art of forming natural conic expressions. The name Hypatia is also associated with a free open-source software license that allows for both free use and commercial distribution of models generated using the package. The package provides three different conversion methods for natural conic expressions and includes tools for validating these expressions and the resulting conic expressions. Several approaches have been explored to develop efficient and dependable MRI data filtering protocols, including statistical methods, machine learning techniques, and hybrid models. However, the effectiveness of these methods depends heavily on MRI scanner stability, leading to challenges in applying them to new scanners. This issue can be addressed by developing robust quality assessment techniques that prioritize generalization. This paper explores the generalizability of MRI data quality assessment models, investigating the impact of specific factors such as scanner change, image enhancement techniques, and preprocessing methods on model performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate a strategy for evaluating and refining models to ensure they perform optimally in novel situations. This research utilizes brain MRI data, but the proposed evaluation framework is applicable to quality assessment problems across all modalities. The proposed methodology provides a quantitative measure of model performance and a score for predictive performance, enabling efficient model selection and further improvement through data inclusion, such as incorporating redundant features or using different learning algorithms. The integration of electric vehicles is becoming increasingly common and is expected to continue this trend. Unfortunately, this growth may lead to an explosion of charging demands during power outages, potentially causing instability in the grid and making recovery operations more challenging. To address this issue, an innovative multi-agent optimization framework is proposed, which utilizes private electric vehicles as sources of energy storage to improve grid resilience. The proposed method considers various aspects, including financing, transportation, energy storage, and grid recovery, to determine optimal charging and dispatch strategies for individual vehicles. By utilizing a mixed-integer linear programming model, the method maximizes the economic benefits of vehicle owners, fills grid knowledge gaps, and meets various constraints. To validate the proposed model, real-world data from California is used in a case study. The results show that optimizing vehicle charging and dispatch during outages can increase recovery costs, but this comes with additional expenses of vehicle operation, maintenance, and equipment. Furthermore, the proposed method falls within the range of existing, unfavourable policies such as net metering. The proposed multi-agent optimization method can be applied to various situations, including power outages, by utilizing EVs as energy storage, and has far-reaching implications for policymakers, vehicle manufacturers, and potential owners. The study also highlights the limited understanding of power outages and the uncertain behaviour of vehicle drivers, suggesting that more comprehensive models and driver behaviour analysis are necessary. The proposed model can be improved by accounting for outages caused by vehicle breakdowns, wind-up, and sudden loss of grid visibility, as well as exploring alternative energy storage solutions, such as solar panels, and the financial and environmental impacts of vehicle breakdowns and grid visibility loss. The results can be validated using real-world data from other regions, and more in-depth case studies involving specific transportation and energy systems. The proposed method and resulting insights can be applied to other energy storage solutions, and the study highlights the significance of considering the complex dynamics of power outages and the interactions between transportation and energy systems. Evaluations of the integrated framework were conducted in various scenarios, including single-agent scenarios with noisy observations and multi-agent meeting scenarios. The results show that DBIM yields superior outcomes when compared to alternative approaches in single-agent scenarios with noisy observations, and the introduction of an incentive curve in multi-agent meeting scenarios leads to more substantial collaborations and faster meeting convergence. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of a novel material, GdCmSn$_3$, and a series of alloys based on it, Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$, using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied all-in-all-out magnetic order existing in the GdCmSn$_3$ compound and found it to be stable. However, we also discovered another all-in-all-out magnetic order possible in this material, with a higher energy state. Furthermore, we found that the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ alloys can exhibit ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic behavior, depending on the Cm content. Our results also indicate that the energy gaps of the XSn$_3$ compounds are very small, classifying them as semiconductors, and that the electronic and magnetic properties share some similarities with the well-known all-in-all-out material, Mn$_3$Sn. Nonetheless, the unique all-in-all-out electronic and magnetic characteristics, coupled with the difficulty of synthesizing GdCmSn$_3$, make this compound and its alloys promising candidates for scientific study. Not to mention their potential utilization in devices such as field-effect transistors, where the all-in-all-out order could be modulated to control the semiconductor-to-metallic transition. The experimental observation of the all-in-all-out order and magnetic transitions in this material and its alloys will require further analysis, possibly involving X-ray diffraction, specific heat measurements, magnetometry, photoemission and absorption spectroscopies. The optimized crystal and magnetic conditions derived from this study can be utilized to investigate the phonons, electron-phonon interactions, and the magnetic field effects on the electronic and magnetic properties of GdCmSn$_3$ and the GdCmSn$_3$ compounds using finite temperature and magnetic field calculations. The magnetic anisotropy present in the magnetic moments and energy gaps makes this material and its alloys suitable for magnetic anisotropy-based effects, all-in-all-out ordered compounds, and the anisotropic Dirac fermions, respectively. The presence of both p and d orbital contributions to the energy gaps in the GdCmSn$_3$ compounds suggests they may exhibit both metal-to-semiconductor and ferromagnetic-to-antiferromagnetic transitions, making this material and its alloys fascinating subjects for scientific study. In this work, extra fields beyond the standard model are investigated to demonstrate that, when completed, the standard model requires an SU(3)xSU(2)xU(1) symmetry to function effectively. We analyze the implications of this requirement on quark and lepton sectors, considering both fundamental and composite extra particles, including mesons made of quarks and leptons. We discuss three main scenarios: one where the extra fields form a set of conformally coupled scalar fields that group extra baryons and mesons together, another that incorporates a pair of Higgs-like fields generating extra baryons and mesons, and a third that involves a two-loop effect arising from a scalar field attached to extra baryons or mesons. We also examine the possibility of extra fields attached to a non-abelian gauge force carrier, such as gluons, electroweak gauge carriers, or a new gauge carrier, and discuss the predictability of these scenarios, including forecasts for future particle acceleration experiments, such as the Future Circular Collider, the Compact Linear Collider, and the International Linear Collider. In particular, we anticipate the discovery of extra baryons or mesons with mass less than 10 TeV, with electric charge greater than 0.01 or magnetic moment greater than 10 times that of the electron, or certain specific mass-to-magnetic-moment ratios. We also provide a set of simplified expressions that can be useful for searching these particles in experimental data. Given the predictability of these scenarios, we propose a research program for the Future Circular Collider, the Compact Linear Collider, and the International Linear Collider that focuses on (1) completing the standard model, (1) investigating the fundamental nature of extra baryons and mesons, (1) exploring the standard model parameter space, (1) searching for extra particles attached to a non-abelian gauge force carrier, and (1) studying forward scattering processes. We anticipate finding evidence of extra baryons or mesons in the first 100 inverse femtobarns of data collected at the Future Circular Collider, with a proposed detector configuration known as the Future Circular Collider Experiment. We also discuss the overlap between these research programs and other experiments, such as top quark production at the Large Hadron Collider, electron-positron colliders, neutrino and cosmic ray experiments, dark matter experiments, and baryon and meson decay at the surface or in the atmosphere. The Coxeter group foundation theorem, initially proven by Bouscaren and Reutenauer, essentially states that a free group is generated by the elements of a Coxeter group if and only if the group's defining mirror reflections all possess infinite order. In this paper, we establish an analogous result for the basis elements of a exchange system associated with a finite irreducible quadratic diagram, specifically Diagram D of Nambu sense, following the format introduced by EiQi SuLi and YuGe Fu. Additionally, we investigate related properties and a significant result of Potocka's, concerning the group Sn(n+2) when n is an odd number greater than 1. Moreover, we establish an alternative proof of Potocka's result, as well as a related open problem. Lastly, we examine the foundation property of a specific class of groups, namely the biparabolic groups, and determine its connection to the Gelfand-Petrov metric. Lastly, we establish an analogue of the Coxeter group foundation theorem utilizing the Gelfand-Petrov metric. Lastly, we establish an analogue of the Coxeter group foundation theorem for the B-type Coxeter groups based on the basis elements of an exchange system associated with a finite irreducible diagram D of Nambu sense, specifically Diagram D of the sn(n+2) group when n is an odd number greater than 1.

Reconstructing cosmological parameters relying on the cosmological evolution of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) rely on mapping their luminosity distortion due to gravitational lensing caused by foreground mass structures. We calculated this effect for the largest SN Ia datasets available, using a simple model that accounts for the statistical properties of SNe Ia and galaxy distributions. Our findings indicate a significant lensing influence in a narrow SN Ia brightness range, and that it correlates with the multiplicity of SNe Ia within a given distance range. Furthermore, we found that lensing's impact can be explained by the distribution of individual galaxies hosting a SN Ia, rather than cosmological principles. Our analysis suggests that the most likely explanation for the SN Ia brightness range and the multiplicity phenomenon lies in the lensing effect caused by the accumulation of SNe Ia within galaxy clusters. However, we also consider alternative explanations involving SN Ia host galaxy properties. Our research utilized the Pantheon SN Ia dataset, with additional data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Galaxy And Mass Assembly survey, to estimate the average lensing effect as one SN ratio of 0.638 ± 0.066, and the most likely explanation for the SN Ia multiplicity phenomenon remaining unknown. Nonetheless, we found that lensing's impact is consistent with its dependence on the density of galaxy clusters, indicating that it may be necessary to reconsider its significance in SN Ia cosmology in light of this finding. Our analysis predicts a comparable estimate of the lensing effect for the SN Ia datasets SN II + SN Ia combined, including the At2019 category, although these estimates require further confirmation. Lastly, we suggest an easy-to-implement modification for future SN Ia cosmology analyses, including a cautionary note about the potential pitfalls of neglecting lensing's impact, which could, in the extreme case of highly overdense galaxy clusters, manifest as a SN Ia population discrepancy similar to the gap between SN Ia and SN II.

We have investigated the fundamental characteristics of T hubs, either with or without a ring at their center, including their mode-count, phase coverage, and compatibility with different branch configurations. Our findings indicate that, by adjusting the geometric parameters of the branches, it is possible to achieve high refractive index sensitivity and mode splitting ratios of up to ten in T hubs. Furthermore, we have observed that a ring-based T hub mode structure can be precisely mimicked by a more straightforward silicon photonic compound structure, referred to as a T-like directional coupling system, which provides a more compact and robust alternative. Our results demonstrate that both T hubs and their associated components are suitable options for implementing optical sensing applications. Our research has also explored the integration of T hubs with waveguides, revealing that a ring-based T hub can be effectively combined with a ring resonator of the same diameter to create a high-q structure with precise mode structure and strong signal differentiation, accompanied by tight phase and amplitude coverage. This paper introduces a novel theory explaining how context affects the recall of abstract objects in deep learning models that recognize objects. Our context assessment technique, accurately assessing context for deep object recognizers (TALES), uses minimal resources and detects which context is most effective at retrieving a specific object class. TALES generates a numerical representation of context's impact on object recognition. We demonstrate this technique's utility by analyzing both naturally occurring and artificially created contexts. Our results show that context's influence can be both positive and negative, and that context that is too complex can sometimes have a negative impact on object recognition. We also examine the relationship between context and the recall of individual objects, revealing that context's impact is unique to each object class. Finally, we explore the connection between TALES and other object recognition evaluation methods, discovering that it provides a distinct perspective on the objects that are easiest or hardest for a model to recognize. We make TALES available to the public in the hope that it will facilitate further research into the complexities of object recognition within deep learning models. The code can be found at https://github.com/PranavGupta/TALES. The paper also includes five additional sections that were rejected by the reviewers: (1) an examination of the representation of context through generative models, (2) a comparison of the effectiveness of different contexts using hard objects to recognize, (3) a study of the relationship between context and the recall of individual objects using simple models, (4) a discussion of the representation of context and the ease of recognizing objects, and (5) a section that presents a graphical representation of the recall of individual objects, and offers some initial intuition about the theory of context and object recognition. We examine the concentration of randomly generated matrices whose entries are drawn from independent and identically distributed distributions. In particular, we derive large-deviation estimates for independent rows of these matrices, yielding new results for moments and characteristic functions. Additionally, we investigate the concentration of binary random variables with dependent distributions, providing general inequalities that can be applied to specific structures such as randomly assembled networks and random matrix ensembles. These inequalities enable us to tackle a variety of linear optimization problems, generating new upper bounds for their expectation and new tail estimates, which can be used to extend recent results from theoretical computer science to broader classes of problems. Our approach also connects discrete sampling to continuous distributions, yielding novel applications of the continuous Talagrand's convex distance inequality to computer science problems. Finally, we show that for certain measures of matrix width, the guarantee we obtain for random matrix ensembles is essentially the same as that for the Gaussian measure, demonstrating that the guarantee we obtain for linear optimization problems is also essentially the same as that for the standard binary distribution, and providing an alternative interpretation of recent results from theoretical computer science. Our main concentration inequality for binary random variables also enables us to extend recent results from theoretical computer science to problems with dependent distributions, providing a general and versatile approach to tackling these problems. In particular, this allows us to solve a question posed by DeLaPena and Levin, extending their approach to ranked enumeration problems. Moreover, this technique can be applied to marked or ranked version of random network ensemble, which includes and extends Erdos's recent result, enabling us to extend further to other models such as random clique assembly. Finally, we derive upper bounds for specific classes of linear optimization problems, providing new and concrete results that can be compared with recent results from theoretical computer science. Our main approach involves a novel combination of independent sampling, a measure called subcode, and a concentration inequality for convex functions, which can be achieved using Talagrand's convex distance inequality, yielding a constant that depends on the distribution and is independent of the size of the random variable. Our results can be applied to a wide range of models and problems, providing a flexible and general approach to tackling linear optimization problems and random variable concentration, which can be used in various areas of computer science and mathematics. The recent introduction of incompatible kidney transplants from living donors has posed significant challenges to implantation strategies. While multiple kidney transplants from the same donor can be syngenic, their recipient matching histories vary greatly, making traditional compatibility assessments inadequate. A new framework is needed to evaluate these donations, considering not just immunological compatibility but also the potential risks to the donor. Here, we propose an ideal standard for accepting such kidneys, striking a balance between minimizing immunological risk for the recipient and protecting the donor's well-being. This standard takes into account factors like kidney donation frequency, post-transplant outcomes for the recipient, and the physical and psychological effects of donation on the donor. Although this concept was initially explored in the context of live donations, its relevance extends to incompatible organs from deceased donors as well. The proposed framework provides a foundation for comparing and selecting the best incompatible kidney transplants for a particular recipient. The recent advancement in kidney transplantation surgery, particularly the development of simultaneous dual kidney transplants without cooling, has significant implications for these assessments. The ideal standard can be refined further by incorporating clinical expertise, ultimately aiming to maximize the benefits of incompatible kidney transplants while minimizing risks to both the recipient and the donor. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word representations learned through the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Dictionary, a widely used resource for capturing the emotional content of words. We establish a mathematical framework to represent words as vectors, incorporate their polarity labels, and experiment with different learning models to demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms standard word2vec and performs optimally in multiple evaluation metrics. However, we also identify limitations in the dictionary that could be hindering the effectiveness of these models. We propose potential solutions to these issues including combining the dictionary with part-of-speech tags, leveraging dictionary-based semantic relatedness, and incorporating syntactic knowledge from graphs of word relationships. We demonstrate the benefits of these approaches on various evaluation metrics. We also explore a more interdisciplinary topic, the representation of words in the Lexicon-Based Semantics framework, and show that incorporating the Loughran-McDonald dictionary's polarity labels as a regularizer leads to better performance in a range of tasks. We make our code available at https://github.com/abdo/word-representation.

This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM schemes that mimic the beneficial consequences of our previously proposed WBWFC structure, leveraging wideband frequency domains to gain additional advantages beyond multiple antennas and carriers. By dividing a wide bandwidth into narrowband signals, these two alternatives also offer data transmission and energy harvesting coexistence, where a low-power receiver can successfully detect signals. SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equate to having multiple antennas and multiple carriers, respectively. However, our results show they outperform their respective SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM counterparts. The proposed structures also tolerate a more significant level of blockage than their single-carrier or single-antenna equivalents. The finding that our schemes are more resilient in blockage scenarios suggests they could be suitable for indoor applications. The proposed SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM structures also support fast data transfer and wireless charging simultaneously. The paper concludes with an analysis of the two schemes, comparing them to the optimal WBWFC, and presenting two special cases that yield new, general results. Furthermore, the paper provides numerical data for various scenarios, presenting the throughputs of the two schemes, WBWFC, SISO-OFDM, and MISO-OFDM. The findings can be applied to various environments, such as outdoor and indoor settings, along with two special cases mentioned above. The paper ends with a discussion of future work and possible generalizations of the two schemes. A key process in mathematical physics, the 2D random log-gas model, describes the behavior of $N$ particles scattered on the circle under the influence of a random potential, and is characterized by a specific Stieltjes transform $\rho$. As $N$ approaches infinity, this leads to the emergence of a continuous density $\rho$ that determines the behavior of the log-gas. We show that the 2D random log-gas is related to a specific Schramm-Loewner evolution, known as the chordal SLE$_\kappa$ process, with $\kappa$ equal to $4(\rho(1)+\rho(-1))$. This connection enables us to couple the time-$t$ log-gas ensemble with the SLE$_\kappa$ process for $0\leq t\leq T$, and to establish that the Asymptotic Decay Theorem holds for a class of initial data. Furthermore, we establish that as $N$ approaches infinity, the log-gas density $\rho_N$ converges to a constant density $\rho$ almost surely, and that this density determines the SLE$_\kappa$ process to which the coupled system asymptotically decays. Finally, we show that there is a critical value $\rho_c$ such that the SLE$_\kappa$ process for $\rho>\rho_c$ asymptotically decays to a straight line, and that $\rho_c$ is equal to $1/2$. In addition, we provide an alternative proof of this statement, as well as an expression for $\rho_c$ in terms of a specific conformal field theory. These results extend to a wide range of random interface models, including many SLE$_\kappa$ processes, and provide a solution to the inverse problem of determining the driving field $\rho$ given the SLE$_\kappa$ process. They also provide a framework for studying these models using the tools of SLE, and offer a potential approach to evaluating physically significant quantities in the context of the 2D random log-gas model. Lastly, we offer a conjecture regarding a specific property of $\rho$, and the possibility of extending our results to a wide range of random interface models driven by $\HP$ measures.

This paper is targeted at a general academic audience interested in the technical aspects of conducting collective research. Understanding the meaning of diverse phrases with different semantics is a challenging aspect of language interpretation.  This study introduces a novel task called Semantic Variety Detection (SVD), which involves identifying phrases exhibiting different semantics from at least one comparison.  Utilizing Natural Language Inference (NLI) data, a resource that is well-suited for capturing semantic variations, we derive three variants of the SVD task and evaluate them using custom scripts and NLI datasets.  Our experiments in multiple languages demonstrate a range of insights, from the significance of considering context in determining semantic diversity to the difficulty of detecting diverse semantics within NLI data.  A substantial portion of the analyzed NLI instances exhibit different semantics when viewed in isolation but become indistinguishable in context, suggesting a strong connection between context, diversity, and NLI decisions.  Ultimately, this research highlights the SVD task as a valuable means of evaluating conversational understanding models and provides a range of pre-trained models suitable for benchmarking this task.  All-related code and data are available at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/Semantic_Variety_Detection.

In measurements involving sensitive amplitude assessments, statistical fluctuations arising from data samples can hinder the detection of substantial shifts resulting from experimental influences.  This issue can be addressed by analyzing the structure of fluctuations in the amplitude under consideration, providing a logical framework for identifying misinterpretations of statistical fluctuations as significant shifts.  This concept can be demonstrated with a specific example involving the measurement of amplitude shifts caused by instrumental effects in proton-proton collision data at the Large Hadron Collider.  A newly introduced quantity, "fluctuation fraction," is introduced as a measure of the extent to which amplitude distributions are affected by instrumental effects, facilitating the detection of shifts resulting from experimental influences.  The relationship between this quantity and traditional statistical measures is explored, along with its utility in displaying amplitude shifts on plots comparing data to theoretical predictions.  The effectiveness of the fluctuation fraction is further illustrated with results from a real experimental analysis, involving instrumental effects in the measurement of the Higgs boson mass in the $bb$ final state with 13 TeV proton-proton collisions.  The results are summarized in tables for easy reference.  The code used to generate these results is available online, offering a practical example for users navigating similar measurements.  The approach discussed in this paper is relevant to a broad range of amplitude measurements and can be applied to other experiments involving sensitive amplitude assessments in collision data.  The development of this analysis was facilitated by the free, open-source HiggsAnalysis/EffectiveProjections package, which provides user-friendly implementations of effective projections, including amplitude shift reweighing, along with useful helper functions.  This package is compatible with standard root files and provides the ability to read and write these files directly.  The code also includes examples of plotting amplitude distributions, comparing data to theoretical predictions, and displaying the fluctuations in amplitude distributions resulting from instrumental effects on plots comparing data to theoretical predictions, in addition to the fluctuation fraction. In the context of graph theory, a key problem is the bipartite vertex division issue, which can be described as follows: given a graph and two color groups, we need to determine the largest number of times a given subgraph of two colored vertices can be subdivided within the graph. This problem has been proven to be computationally difficult to solve for most graph types. In this research, we established an algorithm that can efficiently solve the bipartite division problem in a time acceptable for large input sizes, and demonstrated this approach can be applied to multiple specific graph types. Furthermore, our findings show that this method can also be used to accurately calculate the maximum number of times a specific subgraph can be fully replicated within a given graph. Additionally, our research revealed a significant improvement in the existing time-cost profile for a particular instance of the graph division problem known as the 'hidden clique problem'. This new approach may be used as a component for solving other more complex problems, such as detecting all fully connected subgroups within a given graph. In contrast to this approach, current methods of solving the hidden clique problem typically result in a significant increase in the computational time required. In the course of this research, we also clarified an error in an previously published study regarding the time complexity of the hidden clique problem. In its current form, this algorithm utilizes a branching technique that involves coloring vertices, resulting in a time complexity of O(3^d), where d represents the largest dimension of the subgraph in question. By contrast, the existing method of solving this problem is said to have a time complexity of O(2.715^d). In this work, we introduce a novel attack strategy known as 'Pragmatic Privacy Assaults in Vertical FL' (PPA VF2L), which is designed to compromise the security of vertical federated learning. Users with different data attributes share their information with multiple servers connected by peer-to-peer networks. Our aim is to breach the privacy of a specific server by stealing sensitive information from another user, given that the data of that user is also being shared with that server. To achieve this, we develop an accurate estimation method that determines the quality of sent data, as well as a greedy algorithm to maximize the acquired data attributes. Our experiments show that PPA VF2L can effectively steal information from users with rare data attributes, leading to a drop in model accuracy. Moreover, we demonstrate that PPA VF2L succeeds in stealing credits from specific users, thus it can be utilized as a sampling method to breed robust and secure machine learning models. Our research also identifies potential weaknesses in current VF2L protocols, highlighting the necessity for further security and protocol design analysis. Moreover, we show that PPA VF2L shares striking similarities with other attacks, such as Reverse Attack and Intentional Noise Attack, thus providing a unified framework for various assault strategies. Our attack can be executed under relatively mild assumptions, making PPA VF2L a versatile method with wide applications. Our data theft detection method is also applicable to non-pragmatic attacks like Flash Attack and Coarse Location Attack. Our research underlines the challenges that users face when implementing VF2L due to data heterogeneity, as well as the necessity for suitable protocols that take into account the diverse attributes of user data. Our solution for this issue involves generating random credits that are redistributed periodically in order to prevent data theft and promote data heterogeneity, as well as implementing tougher privacy requirements on users with rare data attributes in order to enhance model accuracy. Our research provides a platform for exploring other pragmatic attacks on VF2L, as well as other applications in other contexts. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengxiangDrive/PPA-VF2L.

Kernel methods in machine learning, particularly kernel ridge regression, rely heavily on efficient storage and computation with kernel matrices. This research focuses on an interesting aspect of kernel matrix computation, specifically the development of a data-dependent kernel estimation framework. We introduce the concept of Random Fourier Traits (RFTs), a connection between Random Fourier Features (RFFs) and the Traits of Special Functions, which serves as a fundamental building block for this framework. We then outline a method to create RFTs from any function whose kernel can be determined, and demonstrate how this process enables the development of a data-dependent kernel estimation technique. This technique outperforms the traditional RFF method while maintaining a comparable level of memory usage, as evidenced by our experiments using datasets Mnist, Covtype, and Higgs. This approach also offers a modifiable platform for developing novel kernel methods, as shown by our development of a single-classifier decision tree using RFTs. We publicly release our code and a user-friendly interface for the RFT-based method at https://github.com/linge-wang/RFT-Kernel. This research was previously known under the title Random Fourier Traits for Kernel Methods.

A new method of managing radio frequency (RF) energy and data in wireless systems is proposed in Switched and Split Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT). The system, which allows for the separate processing of received data and the extraction of energy from RF signals, enables the efficient use of resources and extends the coverage of wireless networks. Network theory has various applications in biology, medicine, and other fields where networks represent interactions and connections between elements. Though most networks have complex structures, simple models like regular and random networks have limited versatility. Research often focuses on scale-free networks, developing analytical models based on degree distribution. However, determining network dynamics' degree distributions following an avalanche or failure of some nodes is a more intricate problem that even basic models can solve. We introduce a new approach to investigate avalanches in networks by dividing the distribution of connections into two distinct parts - a 'trunk' representing the main network structure and 'branches' representing erratic connections. When analyzing the dynamics of a Cayley tree, we find that the branch connections' distribution takes a specific power-law form that varies according to the tree's dynamics. Specifically, we derive three exact expressions for the branch distribution of the N-node Cayley tree under three different dynamics: the Edwards-Shafer model, the Boltzmann model, and the linear response model. These results demonstrate how the branch distribution changes over time and provides a clear understanding of the effects of changing parameters on the network's dynamics. Furthermore, we determine the condition under which the branch distribution becomes a second-order phase transition, accumulating a small number of nodes with extremely high degree. This model can be applied to real networks, such as biological networks, following a failure or an infection outbreak. In such cases, the model reveals the effects of removing some nodes or introducing an infection at specific nodes on the distribution of connections. This in turn can lead to an avalanche that may result in a second-order phase transition, potentially leading to the destruction of the entire network. This finding is particularly notable when comparing it with the famous Barabási-Albert model, which also explains network dynamics but differs from this model in several aspects. This new approach is not only applicable to random networks but can also be used for other complex systems, such as geographical distributions, where the distribution of connections between locations can be analyzed to better understand natural phenomena. This model has various applications in physics, geography, biology, medicine, and sociology, among other fields, and provides a simple yet effective algorithm for analyzing the dynamics of connections in complex systems. This algorithm is based on the central moment approach, which provides a clear and concise method for investigating the dynamics of networks. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on predicting two overlapping faces from a single image, with some portions potentially obscured. This face-to-face alignment enables the construction of a continuous, occlusion-free three-dimensional face model by merging the predicted faces, thus facilitating seamless handling of head orientations and facial obstructions. The proposed architecture, consisting of two encoders and two decoders connected by cross-modal connections, produces two overlapping three-dimensional face maps from a single image, which are then combined to generate a complete and occlusion-free three-dimensional face model. To train this model, we create a dataset with images depicting multiple head orientations and establish a training regimen that simulates various head poses and facial obstructions. Our approach was tested on a dataset tailored to head orientations and on a more general dataset characterized by head poses and facial obstructions, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in comparison to existing methods. The proposed architecture was also evaluated on a benchmark for face annotation and the results show a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art. The code for this research has been made available at: https://github.com/ghristi/SADRNet. The proposed methodology has far-reaching implications for face analysis tasks beyond dense face alignment, such as face anti-synthesis, expression and pose manipulation, and face reconstruction from a single image. The proposed architecture can be enhanced by integrating external knowledge, such as head pose estimation and facial segmention, which has the potential to further improve its performance. The proposed SADRNet architecture has the unique feature of producing two face maps from a single image, which can be combined to generate a single face map, making it an appealing method for face anti-synthesis, face manipulation, and face reconstruction tasks. In an inflationary model, a specific scenario can lead to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs), namely when cosmological perturbations become overly compressed or expanded. We examine the conditions under which this compression or expansion of perturbations can occur in the presence of localized initial fluctuations during an inflationary period. Focusing on a particular class of $\alpha$-attractor inflationary models, we determine the requirements for compressed or expanded perturbations to form over a wide range of fluctuation scales. We also explore the connection between compressed or expanded perturbations and PBH formation. In an analysis of randomized Gaussian fluctuations, we calculate the presssure and density perturbations necessary to compress or expand a significant fraction of the matter density in PBHs. We find that these conditions are met in a narrow range of fluctuation scales. However, when we account for localized initial fluctuations on a wide range of scales, we find that the requirement for compressed or expanded perturbations is easily satisfied. We further determine the presssure and density perturbations necessary to form PBHs with mass coefficients in alignment with LIGO's observations. In a specific inflationary model based on an $\alpha$-attractor slope of $f_{\rm NL} \approx 5.0$, we find that the formation of PBHs with masses detected by LIGO requires a wide range of fluctuation scales. Furthermore, we determine the contribution of these PBHs to the overall energy density in the universe, which falls within the range of predictions based on the cosmic microwave background. We also examine the prediction for the PBH mass spectrum in this model, which indicates a peak mass coefficient of $10.5$ with a broad distribution extending over several orders of magnitude. We further analyze the relation between PBH formation and compressed or expanded perturbations in other $\alpha$-attractor inflationary models based on different slopes of $f_{\rm NL}$. We find that in models with $f_{\rm NL} \lesssim 5$, the compressed or expanded perturbations that form PBHs with masses detected by LIGO are compressed, whereas in models with $f_{\rm NL} \gtrsim 5$, the compressed or expanded perturbations that form PBHs with masses detected by LIGO are expanded. We also determine the PBH mass spectra in these models, which predict a broad distribution of PBH masses based on the fluctuations in the primordial density field.

We define the rootmost vertex with the deepest value as the tree's deepest vertex. Our goal is to analyze the structure of ordered trees based on their highest valued leaves. We have identified three key structures: trees with multiple deepest vertices, and those in which all values are distinct or belong to a sequential range. For the latter two cases, we provide explicit formulas for the number of trees. To evaluate iOCR on this particular dataset, we conducted a series of experiments, starting with a straightforward OCR comparison, and also assessing the system's performance on two critical election-related metrics: candidate name matching and vote tally accuracy. Additionally, we explored the impact of various iOCR parameters on its results, and also examined the potential benefits of using iOCR with strategic sampling methods in order to reduce the cost of human validation processes. A key challenge in the integration of renewable energy sources lies in managing seasonal fluctuations, which can be addressed through advanced storage systems. As storage technology improves, there's a growing interest in self-planning energy and storage independently by individual households. Although various methods exist for optimizing energy consumption across different time periods, most require historical data on prices and temperature fluctuations. Additionally, storage planning models typically assume optimal use of storage capacity in real-time markets. In this study, a decentralized storage planning model is developed that considers the limited information available to households and the optimal use of storage in real-time markets. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated in a case study using data from the German market. The results show that, even with limited information, household storage can be an economic and efficient option, and that its value increases with higher electricity prices and more extensive access to decentralized markets. The research also highlights the importance of accurate price forecasting in household storage planning, and the potential risks associated with centralized decision-making on storage investment, such as market concentration and supply chain disruptions. The study suggests that decentralized storage planning reduces these risks, and allows for more adaptive planning across different time periods. The results further indicate that, with adequate funding, household storage can be an economic and efficient option, and that the most cost-effective approach is typically the "cautious self-planning" method, which prioritizes the optimal use of storage in real-time markets above other considerations. The study concludes by highlighting the broader implications of decentralized storage planning for individual households, and the potential for transferring its principles to other applications, such as supply chain planning, turf management, and gardening. A simplified computer model is used to create a global atmosphere and study the patterns of wind and circulation formed under different rotation rates of the system. By comparing models with various rotation rates, a gradual transition from a fast-winding, super-rotating atmosphere to a slower-winding, more turbulent atmosphere is observed. Through this analysis, researchers identify key factors that influence the formation of atmospheric circulation patterns and examine how they change in response to changes in rotation rate. They also introduce a new method for measuring the speed at which air moves within the atmosphere, finding that a specific range of rotation rates favors atmospheric circulation patterns characterized by fast-moving air near the surface and slower-moving air at higher altitudes. In the second part of this study, the models are modified to include the effects of land heating disparities between the equator and the poles, which results in the formation of unique wind patterns over land, including winds that blow from the ground up in certain regions. This leads to the creation of distinct circulation patterns in these areas, which vary significantly depending on the system's rotation rate. The models also reveal that the development of these patterns is influenced by the height at which atmospheric turbulence occurs and the rate at which air moves within the atmosphere. The application of these models to exoplanetary atmospheres showcases the versatility of these experiments, which can be adapted to study atmospheres on various planets, including those on Mars, four times larger, as well as terrestrial planets like Earth. Our proposed "dynamic learning" technique tackles issues related to large-scale neural network training, specifically focusing on the challenges of efficient data preprocessing and optimal model updating. We show that by utilizing a separate neural network to identify and target specific data classes, we can significantly enhance the effectiveness of our dynamic learning approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this technique can be applied to various tasks, including classification, regression, and anomaly detection, and even enable seamless model updates without knowing the exact distribution of the new data. We have tested "dynamic learning" on several benchmarks and real-world scenarios and have found it to be highly successful. Our code is now available on GitHub at the specified URL. We have also submitted a longer version of this paper to publication review. The challenges we sought to address in this work are common in various contexts, including, but not limited to, autonomous systems, smart homes, and medical imaging, where data is continually being collected and the model needs to be regularly updated to maintain its level of accuracy. The technique we have proposed provides a foundation for further research and we have outlined some potential directions in the appendix. However, successful creation of these contacts under certain alignment of the electric and magnetic fields allowed us to observe the conductance of a single quantum channel. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), base stations can adjust their transmission schedules independently to accommodate varying traffic demands, but this leads to interference between the uplink and downlink channels and complicates routing and scheduling decisions. To address this challenge, a new routing, scheduling, and TDD scheduling design has been developed to minimize the finished jobs of tasks by modeling the problem as a non-convex stochastic dynamic multi-player game, yet providing an efficient algorithm to find a distributed strategy that approximates the optimal routing, scheduling, and TDD scheduling solutions. Furthermore, the proposed framework has been evaluated and shows comparable performance to a centralized optimizer, while reducing data loss and improving throughput in various scenarios. The proposed framework has been implemented on real hardware, with results confirming the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed scheduling protocol. In this work, we aim to gain insight into the underlying mechanisms of Hamiltonian Neural Networks by examining whether it is possible to approximate gradient signals using these networks. Our investigation involves analyzing HNN in the context of stochastic gradient descent, and we derive a expression that allows us to interpret the networks as simulating gradient descent. However, this expression can be rearranged to provide a new perspective on HNN, viewing it as a statistical approximation of the distribution of states resulting from gradient descent. This revised understanding challenges a previous interpretation of HNN by Rezende and Vinyals, who described the networks as capturing the dynamics of gradient descent. We also demonstrate that HNN can be viewed as a model for the state distribution following gradient descent, and this perspective has utility in extracting meaningful information from the networks. Furthermore, we discover that in the course of training, the networks initially learn to capture the structure of the data, which over time is supplanted by the learning dynamics. This is reflected in a decrease in the ELBO score, and we validate our findings through the use of a simple experimental simulation. We believe that this analysis provides a valuable contribution to the understanding of HNN and may also serve as a useful tool for troubleshooting and validating these networks. Lastly, we identify a potential relationship between HNN and normalizing flows, and this connection gives rise to further possible future research directions. We conclude by outlining three particular research pathways that emerge from this investigation. This work was previously published in the journal Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) in 2019 under the title "Can we acquire gradients by Hamiltonian Neural Networks?". Simply putting, our method allows a team of artificial agents to collaborate with a human for a common goal that involves assessing the reliability of machine learning models by classifying data. These agents are designed to learn from experience and can determine which model predictions are trustworthy based on past performance. They present the human with data that may have inconsistent labels, and ask for confirmation of the predicted classification. The reliability ratings provided by the human in response help the agents to refine their ability to anticipate which predictions are reliable without further input from the human. This information is then used to eliminate data that is easily classified and instead focus on data that is more difficult to label accurately, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the process. The goal of this process is to provide better training for machine learning models by accumulating a more comprehensive and diverse dataset of data that has been accurately labeled for reliability. The approach behind our method can be applied to a variety of tasks that involve human judgment to validate the reliability of data and correct inconsistencies in labels. The proposed method was tested on multiple datasets and compared to existing methods, and also combined with existing transfer learning techniques for additional improvement. The results show significant enhancements over existing methods in terms of classification accuracy, reliability rating accuracy, and the efficiency of the process. Word Sense Discrimination (WSD) aims to determine the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings based on its context.  Advances in deep learning, especially BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with a particular focus on combining context representations with gloss information to improve sense prediction.  However, using gloss information in this way has several limitations, including the requirement for extensive knowledge bases and the difficulty of incorporating them into models.  To address these challenges, this research introduces a novel strategy that enhances context representations using a gloss-driven approach, either by re-weighting existing context vectors or producing new vectors, and evaluates different methods to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.  The results show that both re-weighting and producing new vectors using gloss information can significantly improve the performance of BERT in WSD tasks, and the best-performing model, a re-ranking method, demonstrates a significant improvement of 6.3% in F1-score compared to the BERT-base baseline when using the SenseVal dataset.  To further validate this approach, the research also examines a real-world application involving Wikipedia knowledge bases to demonstrate that context-gloss enhancement can be effective in resolving semantic ambiguity in texts.  The associated code has been made available at: https://github.com/saleem-dilawar/ContextGloss-ENHANCE.

This study forms the basis of a comprehensive exploration. It introduces a set of integral definitions for the reciprocal gamma function, which includes a formal introduction of the regularized gamma function and several of its variations, including a generalized and an extended version of the 1940 Watson's formula. Furthermore, established and novel integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function are examined, and new expressions derived from hypergeometric functions are presented. Additionally, this study shows that the regularized gamma function can be expressed as the coefficient of a term in a series expansion, and obtains a general integral representation of this function. Lastly, this research provides a specific example of an integral representation of the reciprocal gamma function and establishes its connection to the hypergeometric function based on a specific integral representation of the regularized beta function. To address the problem of distinguishing quark generations through the top quark in proton-nucleus collisions, we examine potential obstacles and explore possible solutions. Due to the difficulty in accurately measuring the rapidity of the leading b-quark, determining the origin of the second b-quark in events featuring two b-jets and one jet is particularly challenging. We discuss various factors influencing this scenario, including the scattering of one b-quark off a parton within the nucleus, and highlight the crucial role of accurate b-quark rapidity measurement in resolving this ambiguity. Furthermore, we investigate the utility of proton-proton data as a reference, showcasing how the top-quark enriched sample predicted by certain models can be distinguished from background through the characteristics of same- or opposite-charge same-azimuth $\Bmeson$ pairs. To this end, we establish a new, top-quark generation-specific observable: the ratio of same- to opposite-charge same-azimuth $\Bmeson$ pair distributions, which demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying the origin of the second b-quark in events featuring two b-jets and one jet. Additionally, we explore the potential of this ratio to the underlying physics of the process, presenting it in a form readily applicable to numerical evaluation. Moreover, we examine the distinct rapidity distributions of the leading and subleading b-quarks in events featuring one b-jet and $\Bmeson$ pairs, and investigate how the mass of the additional quark could be deduced from the characteristics of such pairs, primarily through the use of $\Bpmesons$ systems. Lastly, we discuss the generality of our findings, emphasizing that this approach is applicable to the detection of any four-quark process. This study focuses on key elements in interpreting and executing SQL queries, specifically the analysis of text based on relational models, using knowledge gained from large language models, with the goal of developing a standalone, end-to-end SQL execution framework from raw text inputs. To enhance the efficacy of this framework, additional tasks such as text classification and natural language generation are incorporated to fine-tune the underlying relational knowledge, but these tasks are eliminated in a cross-domain setting where there are no associated text labels available. This issue is addressed by introducing a strategy that maintains the efficacy of the framework in the absence of text labels. Experimental evaluations in a cross-domain setting showcase the superiority of our approach over rival methods. Moreover, an evaluation in a setting with available text labels for training reveals that our approach can effectively make use of this additional information, thereby outperforming other comparison methods. The resulting execution accuracy in both settings also surpasses that of other comparison methods, including those utilizing massive amounts of background data without the need for text labels. The code along with model weights are available at GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/TextSQL-AutoExec.

Consider a text corpus from the English language, along with a distance function, and apply the FPE model to obtain a scaling factor that yields approximately natural language frequencies for any given distance function. This scaling factor can be thought of as a smooth, varying frequency function, which in turn enables the development of a family of large alphabet size asymptotic deviation principles. These principles quantify the distance between a Markov chain of increasing alphabet size and a specific stationary process, both governed by the rules of natural language. Specifically, our findings establish that for any given distance function, the sum of the absolute differences between the corresponding frequencies of a Markov chain and a stationary process is asymptotically proportional to the square root of the alphabet size. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the existence of a family of distance functions for which the sum of the absolute differences between the corresponding frequencies of a Markov chain and a stationary process remains constant and equal to 1, despite the process's correlation properties. Our work also proves that the asymptotic deviation principles hold globally, i.e., they hold for the entire set of correlated letter sequences, as well as for the distribution of sums of localized terms, i.e., the frequency distributions of words within a text. Our methods involve a novel application of large alphabet size asymptotic renewal theory, a new formulation of the Euler-Mac Laurenthal method, a parameter that represents correlated language's complexity, and a new classification of distance functions into three categories: those that result in a Markov chain's frequencies' being either constantly equal to 1, or asymptotically proportional to the square root of the alphabet size, or otherwise exhibiting a $\sqrt{\delta}$-behavior.
