In tackling the constraints of numerical relativity, researchers have faced challenges in creating suitable codes to solve the full system of general relativity coupled with a specific model for a collapsing or expanding universe. Any such code must meet two key requirements: first, it must generate solutions that conform to the laws of general relativity, and second, it must ensure that the code can be accurately evolved from an initial guess. To overcome these obstacles, a number of approaches have been explored, such as using conformally flat gauge, combining numerical and analytical components, and implementing semi-analytical methods to solve the system in its early stages. Our novel technique, the Cauchy-Characteristic Initial Value Problem in the Tetrads-Killing vector formulation, offers a distinct pathway with the potential to address fundamental challenges in the field. By leveraging a specific gauge that combines the advantages of both conformally flat and harmonic gauges, this method enables the development of codes capable of evolving the system from a set of complex gauge conditions. Our execution of the technique for a broad range of applications, including the simulation of gravitational waves generated in the merger of black holes and neutron stars, has been successful. The resulting code, AKEGA, delivers accurate solutions when the system is close to a stable state and offers a valuable means of exploring the boundary between which collisions are stable and which are not. The challenges we overcame in developing this code provide a valuable contribution to the broader community, with applications extending beyond the specific case of the CTTK technique. The code we created, AKEGA, is written in the C++ language and includes a range of features, such as the use of the shared memory model, the implementation of the BFGS optimization algorithm, and the inclusion of the Weyl scalar in the gauge, all of which can be used by other researchers working with similar numerical relativity problems. The comprehensive dataset we obtained, featuring the detailed characteristics of the waves generated in the collapse of both black holes and neutron stars, is also available for use by the wider community. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN layers, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We observe an unusual Hall coefficient and anomalous Nernst coefficient ratio in Mn$_3$NiN thin layers, differing from theoretical predictions based on the Zener-Rashba effect and the Komura rule. This unusual ratio can be shifted towards a expected value of 1 through the application of a lateral pressure or strain, allowing the anomalous Nernst effect to be manipulated and potentially enabling the extraction of crucial magnetic layer information. Moreover, our research demonstrates that Mn$_3$NiN materials hold considerable promise for widespread study, offering unique insights into the anomalous Nernst effect and the associated thermal field behavior. Lastly, our work opens up possible avenues for investigating the anomalous Nernst effect in other antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials, providing a framework that can be adapted for these materials by identifying the key parameters relevant to Mn$_3$NiN.

The significant increase in computing requirements for artificial intelligence, despite its historical association with local processing, is evident in the needs of modern applications including real-time video analysis, language translation for video conferencing, and advanced robotics control. This trend poses a problem for the flexibility of existing computing infrastructures, relying on remote services that can result in performance issues, lag, and limited accessibility. This work presents a framework addressing these challenges by enabling the deployment of remote user centers for large-scale collaborative activities. Leveraging a hybrid approach that combines cloud and edge computing, these centers allow multiple users to engage in high-throughput activities simultaneously, while gaining a localized experience. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework with a real-world implementation of a hybrid AI cluster at the University of California, Los Angeles, featuring a 20-node Linux cluster and a 64-node NVIDIA DGX-20 cluster, and report on various performance evaluations of both individual nodes and the overall cluster. The developed framework is suitable for a broad range of applications including data analytics, machine learning, and AI-based tasks, and provides a practical solution for user centers in settings such as remote workspaces, student competitions, and start-up businesses. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/kuoruan/remote-user-center.

Advanced composite materials known as shape-memory polymer composites have unique properties that enable them to absorb and dissipate impact energy through significant deformation before losing their structural integrity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a real-world scenario involving a particular type of composite material subjected to impact loads within an aircraft cabin. We also investigate the practical use of this method for design purposes by analyzing the distribution of damage types and electrical impedance changes across multiple genetic scenarios and provide actionable recommendations to aircraft manufacturers on how to design higher-performance composite materials using this method. In this paper, we demonstrate how metric coefficients in a tensor representation of Euclidean space can be determined using geometric measures. A concise formula is derived to calculate these coefficients. Specifically, it is shown that the metric coefficients in a tensor representation of Euclidean space can be expressed in terms of scalar invariants derived from the Ricci tensor and the Riemann tensor. Furthermore, we establish that these metric coefficients are equal to the square of geometric measures. This conclusion is illustrated with the metric coefficients of a Euclidean space defined in terms of geometric measures. In general, it is shown that the metric coefficients of a Euclidean space can be determined using the formula $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij} r^2$ where $r$ is the geometric measure. It is also demonstrated that the metric coefficients of a Euclidean space can be determined using the formula $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij} e^{2h}$ where $h$ is another type of geometric measure. In both cases, it is shown that the metric coefficients are equal to the square of these geometric measures. This is further illustrated with the example of a flat spacetime metric. In this case, we have the formula $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij} e^{2h_i}$ where $h_i$ are four separate geometric measures. On the other hand, if we have the formula $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij} r^2$, then we have the relation $r = e^h$. Therefore, the two types of geometric measures $r$ and $h$ are closely related, as they differ by a constant factor. This is further discussed in the conclusion. In the conclusion, we also discuss the relationship between the geometric measures and the scalar curvature of a Euclidean space. Specifically, we show that the scalar curvature $\kappa$ can be expressed in terms of the geometric measures as $\kappa = 2 \left( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^i} \right) \left( \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^i} \right) = 2 \left( \frac{\partial r}{\partial x^i} \right) \left( \frac{\partial r}{\partial x^i} \right) / r^2$. This means that the scalar curvature $\kappa$ is equal to twice the square of the gradient of the geometric measures. This conclusion is illustrated with the example of a flat spacetime metric

We investigate the appearance of bosons that weigh less than 13.4 MeV and mediate taste-changing interactions between quarks, potentially offering insights into the underlying causes of flavors seen in particle physics. We focus on a specific interaction where a light boson transforms up or down quarks into charm or bottom quarks, or vice versa. To understand the stability of these bosons, we study their decay processes, considering their possible roles in explaining certain phenomena seen in heavy flavor particle production and their potential connection to recently observed anomalies in certain processes. We find that a particular arrangement of flavor-changing interactions could explain some heavy flavor particle patterns, yet it necessarily leads to the boson's instability. Nevertheless, if we limit the boson's interaction to a single flavor change, we find it's possible these particles could have masses as low as 0.01 eV, forcing us to reconsider certain particle physics phenomena that were previously assumed to be caused by interactions involving much heavier particles. In such cases, these low-mass bosons could influence coherent light scattering and affect some neutron physics processes, whereas more massive bosons, exceeding the 10 MeV threshold, would primarily influence hadron physics processes. We also explore the implications of these interactions for certain particle physics phenomena that were previously unconnected, such as the study of taste-changing interactions in neutron physics and the potential connections to some anomalous processes observed in particle accelerators. We propose several experimental tests to verify the presence of these taste-altering bosons, utilizing existing particle beams and sensors, and provide a rough estimate of the required overall energy for creating these particles in laboratory experiments. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting the potential connections between these results and open questions in particle physics, such as the source of flavor, the stability of particles like the charm quark, and the underlying causes of certain processes seen in particle physics experiments. We suggest several approaches to directly address these issues, including the creation of new experiments designed to detect taste-changing interactions and particles that behave in similar ways, and the analysis of data from existing experiments that could already contain relevant information. We also explore the relationships between these results and related phenomena in physics, such as the influence of taste-changing interactions on particle physics processes in astrophysical settings, the behavior of particles at high temperatures that generate flavor-changing interactions, and the aspects of condensed matter physics that involve flavor-changing interactions and complex material properties. We conclude by providing a summary of the main results, discussing the underlying principles and approaches used in this research, and highlighting the connections between these

The Toda algebras can be characterized by a set of identity operators known as Ward identities, which are derived from the operator product expansion and conformal invariance. In this paper, the structure of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda algebras is examined in detail. The $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda algebras contain both local bulk and boundary operators. The Toda algebras applicable to boundary conditions can be determined by examining the transformation properties of the vertex operators under the Lorentz transformation. The Sp(6, $\mathbb{R}$) Lie algebra, which forms the basis of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda algebras, is implemented through a set of first-order differential operators in the vertex operator construction. We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. This conveys that these lattices have finitely many conjugacy classes of torsion elements. Moreover, this leads to the conclusion that they contain a subgroup isomorphic to a biautomatic group with finite index. Finally, by extending the concept of biautomaticity to graph groups, we show that a specific class of graph groups are biautomatic, resulting in the finite number of conjugacy classes of torsion elements within their lattices, and ultimately, a subgroup isomorphic to a biautomatic group with finite index. This in turn implies that these lattices have a specific 2-group structure, and enables us to precisely count the number of conjugacy classes of torsion elements within them. This further extends to the calculation of the number of conjugacy classes of a specific form within the lattice, allowing us to determine its rank. Lastly, this is demonstrated through explicit examples. The paper at large builds upon the preceding work of Bestvig, Davis, and Drutu, and the fundamental concept of biautomaticity on graph groups was initially discovered by Bestvig. The main contribution here involves generalising the conjugacy class calculation for a specific form of torsion elements within uniform lattices. The paper at large is organised as follows: chapter 2 provides an overview of the key terms and concepts employed throughout the paper; chapter 3 demonstrates that Coxeter groups are biautomatic; chapter 4 explores the implications of this for uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings; chapter 5 examines the concept of graph groups and calculates the number of conjugacy classes of a specific form within uniform lattices; and chapter 6 applies this general concept to a range of lattice examples. The paper at large ends with an appendix containing supplementary material. The main contributors to the paper at large are Bestvig, whose work provided the foundation for the theory presented, and the first name author, who generalised the conjugacy class calculation for a specific form of torsion elements within uniform lattices. The second name author's role was minimal and consisted of providing a discussion on group theory and explaining the concept of biautomaticity. The paper at large was written in 2023. The paper at large is dedicated to the memory of the late professor, Marc Burger

Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body recovery but have yet to achieve successful restoration of lower body mobility with the exception of some level of control over walking devices. To overcome this limitation, a better comprehension of the central mechanisms underlying ambulation is necessary. In this study, we recorded the electrocorticogram (ECoG) activity of partially paralysed rats during guided walking on a treadmill to investigate how movement frequency affects cortical activity and influence brain signals that guide steps. The results revealed that the frequency of walking corresponds to specific ECoG states characterized by distinct oscillatory patterns, and that the corresponding signals could be utilised to predict step frequencies with considerable accuracy. Our findings provide a crucial foundation for the development of effective BCIs capable of predicting step frequencies and restoring lower body mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. The open-source code for this study is available at https://github.com/neuromotionlab/Treadmill-BCI. The findings mentioned in this report have been published in the journal Scientific Reports volume 12, article number 16434 (2022). In this paper, a novel method is introduced that uses neural networks to detect changes in time series components' connections, allows for missing data, and provides a continuous connectivity measure. Furthermore, this approach can be used for forecasting time series by incorporating the estimated connectivity, and it has been shown that this method outperforms the benchmark model in various scenarios. Animals play a significant role in various ecological processes, requiring their geographical tracks to be identified and analyzed. While camera traps provide a valuable source of information for tracking wildlife, the automated detection of biological movement from trapped camera footage remains an unsolved problem. This issue is particularly challenging due to the high frequency of false positives, as shown in Figure 1, which illustrates the false biological detection alerts in Nepal's Annapurna region over the course of a year. To address this challenge, we developed a method that leverages spatial information to distinguish between stationary animals and biological movement. This approach involves a two-part analysis, consisting of a gap detection module that identifies potential biological movement and a filter module that differentiates between genuine and fraudulent movements based on various criteria, including the distance traveled, speed, and animal duration. We evaluated our method on data from Nepal, Zambia, and Madagascar, yielding precision, recall, and F1-score values of 96\%, 39\%, and 56\% respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting genuine biological movement and the necessity of improving its recall to enhance the efficiency of wildlife surveillance. Networks with random defects can convey information reliably, maintaining integrity in the presence of disorder, by utilizing the protective properties of topological phases. Based on 2D time-independent Dirac equations and representing defects as random magnetic fields with contrasting behaviors in different parts of the network, we simulate random binary imperfections to investigate topological phases and conductance. Calculations show that certain random patterns of defects lead to the formation of topological interfaces, allowing for directed information flow and identifying areas where information can safely travel without obstacles. Furthermore, we find that networks with random binary imperfections can exhibit the protection of massless Dirac points, displaying both topological and bulk gap phases in a dependant manner. To accomplish this, we implemented a tight-binding model in a square lattice network and analyzed its topological characteristics using a bulk boundary zigzag method, concluding that networks with random binary imperfections possess the capability to exhibit both topological and bulk gap phases simultaneously. This research was theoretical in nature, conducted using numerical simulations. If realized, "Topological Anderson Networks" could provide unprecedented levels of protection against disorder and topological phases in a range of applications, spanning sound waves in materials to genetic sequences in biology. This study has far-reaching implications, offering potential answers to long-standing questions posed in various fields, and presenting a groundbreaking concept that can be applied to a wide range of contexts. This concept, dubbed Topological Anderson Conductors, represents a novel approach that can be realized in physical systems, such as photonic, acoustic, and genetic systems, among others. This research can be extended to harmonic time-dependent cases and real-space renormalization group methods, offering a richer and more complex understanding of topological phases and conductance. This study has further implications for harmonic and steady flow cases, revealing topological phases that can persist in chaotic flows, both steady and time-dependent, and for genetic sequences, representing a theoretical framework that can be applied to harmonic and steady flows, among other contexts. This research has significant value for various fields, spanning physics, biology, and mathematics, and provides a theoretical framework for analyzing and understanding Topological Anderson Networks in harmonic and steady flows, among other scenarios. The concept of trims emerges from the need to extend the characteristic property of characteristic functions in Boolean lattices. Specifically, a map $f$ has this property if it preserves "at least one" and "at most one" operations. Generalizing, a map that preserves "exactly one" operation for each element in a Boolean lattice can be called a trim. Our investigation into trims reveals they are necessarily isomorphisms, thereby recreating the characteristic property of characteristic functions. Furthermore, a particular classification of trims is presented, demonstrating that any trim is either a composition of a characteristic function and an automorphism, or it is equivalent to a standard, well-known map. This study also touches on the relationship between trims and isomorphisms, highlighting that trims can be viewed as a way to "locally" define an isomorphism within a lattice. A trim can be realized from an isomorphism $\phi$ by selecting a non-zero coefficient $c$ and defining the map $f_x = c\phi(x)$ for each element $x$ in the lattice. This approach ensures that the absolute value of $f_x$ remains equal to the absolute value of the coefficient $c$, thereby ensuring $f$ preserves the operations of the lattice. This interpretation of trims also allows us to explore more general forms of maps that preserve operations, as well as providing a framework for defining and distinguishing between different types of isomorphisms within a lattice. This research was initially presented at the 2015 meeting of the Association for Symbolic Logic.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation involving intricate quantum field theory, specifically the calculation of mass spectra and decay modes for Higgs bosons within the minimal supersymmetric standard model, characterized by complex masses and couplings. A sophisticated technique known as unitary gauge has been employed to ensure the accuracy of these calculations by bypassing the complication of massive gauge boson masses. The resulting expression for massless gauge boson masses relies on complex mass and coupling parameters, making it a comprehensive set of equations that encompasses both tree-level and leading logarithmic two-loop corrections. The analysis also examines decay modes of Higgs bosons, with a focus on the most significant processes involving fermions, as well as the calculated values of massless gauge boson masses at the two-loop level. The development of a dedicated computer program, in the form of a Fortran file, is presented to facilitate calculations for researchers. The underlying methodology and theoretical framework of these calculations are rooted in the minimal supersymmetric standard model, making them applicable to all possible scenarios of the model. The calculation of massless gauge boson masses at the two-loop level marks a significant advancement in the field, while the accuracy of these calculations is continually improved with the emergence of new experimental data. The inclusion of leading logarithmic effects from massless particle loops also expands the scope of these calculations to scenarios characterized by large electroweak gauge symmetry breaking. The development of a comprehensive and highly configurable computer program, written in the Fortran 90 language, allows users to input various sets of mass and coupling parameters to generate the necessary equations for massless gauge boson masses, as well as decay modes of Higgs bosons, with the option to utilize either the 'f freeze' or 'h freeze' scenario. The program is capable of simulating all possible scenarios of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, with a particular focus on the 'large alpha' scenario characterized by complex mass and coupling parameters, making it a highly versatile tool for the field. The calculation of massless gauge boson masses at the two-loop level in the minimal supersymmetric standard model represents a landmark achievement, with all necessary equations and the computer program provided as appendices to the presentation. In contextual linear gambits with $d$ dimensions, agents make decisions based on contextual information and learn a linear decision rule. The contextual parameters and rule coefficients are learned using stochastic gradient descent. We analyze a distributed learning model where multiple agents, located in different nodes of a network, share decision-making responsibility and learn the contextual parameters and rule coefficients independently. We show that, using a communication protocol involving contextual estimates and rule updates, agents at different nodes can jointly determine the contextual parameters and rule coefficients through repeated interactions. This protocol ensures that the learning process converges at a rate of $O(1/t)$, where $t$ denotes the number of iterations. This rate of convergence is achieved without sharing the contextual data, making this result relevant for settings where data privacy is a concern. We also explore a decentralized learning scheme based on a combination of stochastic gradient descent and a gossip algorithm, which enables agents to learn the contextual parameters and rule coefficients in parallel. This scheme leads to a convergence rate of $O(1/t^{1/3})$ in certain special cases. We further examine a model where agents learn a single parameter rather than a vector, which includes contextual linear gambits as a special case. In this model, we show that a decentralized average consensus framework leads to a convergence rate of $O(1/t^{1/3})$ when the degree of the graph underlying the network is bounded, and a convergence rate of $O(1/t^{1/2})$ when the graph is complete. This leads to a convergence rate of $O(1/t^{1/2})$ for contextual linear gambits when the dimension of the context is known and equals $1$. When the dimension of the context is unknown, we show that a variant of the algorithm leads to a convergence rate of $O(\sqrt{t})$ for the vector norm and a convergence rate of $O(d\sqrt{t})$ for the matrix norm in the space of context dimensions. This variant is based on a combination of stochastic gradient descent and a Gibbs estimator, which enables us to handle contextual linear gambits with an unknown dimension of the context. This result is relevant for settings where the dimension of the context is difficult to estimate and learning rates for the matrix norm are typically used. Our research involves examining the underlying assumptions of the event form encoding approach, which converts raw collision data into events for subsequent analysis, specifically for our study of elliptic flow patterns in high-energy lead-lead collisions. To investigate the impact of event encoding, we developed an alternative method based on pseudo-rapidity, without separating encoded events or assuming uniform particle distribution. Our analysis focuses on encoded events from the ALICE experiment and offers a straightforward statistical model to interpret results. Our findings regarding encoded events include: they align with the radial flow pattern, exhibit little change when adjusting encoding parameters, and demonstrate limited influence from encoding assumptions. Notably, our research demonstrates that detailed knowledge of event encoding is unnecessary to analyze encoded data, and we suggest using pseudo-rapidity encodings standard for most analyses. Additionally, our study confirms earlier observations regarding particle distribution patterns and offers a clear view of how event encoding influences such analyses. Lastly, our results indicate that the average number of produced particles can be obtained from encoded data, along with an associated uncertainty. Our approach also provides a basic framework for investigating other event form engineering aspects of collision data. To facilitate further analysis, we have made our code available publicly. Our research was conducted using data from the ALICE experiment obtained during lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV energy level. Our findings stem from approximately 12 million recorded collision events. Our results include detailed graphs plotting encoded particle distributions against pseudo-rapidity, as well as detailed statistical information regarding encoded events, which can be found in separate appendices. Our research provides a foundation for re-engineering event forms, which could involve re-examining the collision data or modifying encoding assumptions, and offers guidelines for investigating other event form encoding aspects of collision data. Our approach offers a straightforward statistical model that can be applied to other analyses of encoded events, along with detailed graphs and statistical information regarding encoded particle distributions and average particle production, which can be found in the data files appended to this document. This work investigates the extremal values of the generalization degrees of freedom (GDoF) benefit that accrues to optimal power control versus binary power control in interference networks with an increasing number of users. Unlike current methods that separate the simulation of particle positions and velocities, this approach combines the two steps and integrates the equations of motion over a variable time period that reflects the duration of actual collisions. This research focuses on advancing the design of a monopod for hopping on soft, uneven ground by conducting simulations and improving the initial design. The aim is to explore the feasibility of a monopod for hazardous terrain sampling through hopping motion. The project assumes a small amount of information is available about the environment and imposes several technical constraints on the design. These simulations utilized the Finite Element Method to model the ground and Euler-Lagrange equations to model the robot. To validate the hard ground controller, a physical monopod was built and used to hike on a hard ground surface. Quantum annealing within a suitable interval can lead to successful outcomes, however, the beginning of this interval is not clear.  This study demonstrates that by comparing classical and quantum quench trajectories, one can determine the quantum annealing interval, thereby providing a vital metric to assess the effectiveness of quantum annealing.  A theoretical analysis is performed to investigate the relationship between this interval and various parameters in the Quantum Annealer, Quench trajectories in the Ising anytime algorithm, and the Verifier-Helfer algorithm in the Exact Cover problem.  The results show that the interval increases as the quantum annealing speed is decreased, the quantum coherence is increased, or the number of quantum annealing intervals is decreased.  A critical point exists in the quench trajectories where the success probability drops dramatically, and this point lies within the interval for a range of noise levels.  The study also highlights the importance of the quench dynamics on the Verifier-Helfer algorithm, and the significance of suitable initial conditions on the quantum annealing outcome.  The findings can be applied to actual Quantum Annealers, such as the D-Wave 2000Q, D-Wave 2000Q Adv, and the Quantum Annealer Sabre XA, etc.  The research focuses on the exact cover problem, however, the study's conclusions are relevant to a broad range of combinatorial optimization problems.  The study utilizes a new metric called the Quantum Annealing Interval, which compares the quantum annealing outcome to the classical quench trajectory, and provides a straightforward and effective way to assess the effectiveness of Quantum Annealing. Our study examines the challenge of achieving high-temperature stability in correlated oxides with a d-orbital arrangement, specifically focusing on nickelate materials. To better understand this challenge, we developed a dual-band model to simulate the energy levels of $d_{\sigma}$ and $d_{\pi}$ orbits, which are essential for capturing screening and stability in these materials. By investigating how the distance between energy bands affects screening and affects the stability, we found that a relatively large distance is necessary to prevent electron coupling and ensure high-temperature stability. However, due caution, we suggest this finding be subject to verification through further research, potentially using advanced numerical methods to ensure its robustness. If confirmed, this result implies that doping the $d_{\sigma}$ band while leaving the $d_{\pi}$ band undisturbed could be a successful approach to achieving high-temperature stability in these materials. We also analyzed a previously reported nickelate material and found that its energy levels are too closely spaced, which may be responsible for its lack of screening and resulting instability. On the other hand, we demonstrated that doping the $d_{\pi}$ band while modifying the $d_{\sigma}$ band to increase the distance between energy levels can lead to improved screening and stability in this material. Furthermore, we analyzed a hypothetical compound made of lanthanum nickelate and showed that it exhibits both screening and stability, which could be achieved by doping the $d_{\pi}$ band while modifying the $d_{\sigma}$ band to increase the distance between energy levels. This approach is supported by both theoretical calculations and experimental information obtained through X-ray scattering. This result suggests that this approach could also succeed in achieving high-temperature stability in other materials with a d-orbital arrangement, specifically focusing on the (dx,dπ) bands in other 4d and 5d oxides. This study provides a basic understanding of the challenge of achieving high-temperature stability in these materials and provides a theoretical framework for resolving this challenge. We also demonstrated that reducing the dimensionality of these materials from two-dimensional layers to one-dimensional chains or zero-dimensional points can lead to achieving high-temperature stability without screening, which may be applicable to implementing this approach in practice. We concluded by analyzing a hypothetical compound made of gadolinium nickelate and found that it exhibits both screening and stability, which could be achieved by doping the $d_{\pi}$ band while modifying the $d_{\sigma}$ band to increase the distance between energy levels. We investigate a variety of quantum states made up of multiple modes, examining how squeezing and phase shifting affect their compass properties. Quantifying the compass nature of these states is achieved by analyzing their overall quantum content alongside specific mode-specific quantum contents. Our research reveals that coherent states with certain squeezing and phase shifting exhibit unique behavior, existing at specific squeezing values where the compass properties switch abruptly. Additionally, our study finds that certain states can be assembled from individual modes with distinct compass characteristics, thereby demonstrating mode-reconstructible states. Our findings also highlight specific state properties, such as uniform quantum contents across all modes, or specific mode-specific quantum contents, which can be manipulated through squeezing and phase shifting. Our analysis serves as a foundation for exploring generated states with various quantum parameters, offering valuable insights into the interplay between squeezing, phase shifting, and compass properties, and providing a basis for discussing the implications of our results on continuous-variable compass state protocols. Our work is further complemented by a relevant discussion on the relationship between coherent states, as well as the scattering of these states on the Fock space. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in the distant regions of young star disks, which could contribute to spreading particles and reducing the VSI may result in an uneven distribution of solids. To understand the effect of particle accumulation on VSI, we examined the VSI in lab-scaled simulations containing varying levels of particles, focusing on areas far from the star where VSI typically occurs. The development of particles was observed to enhance the VSI over a wide range, causing them to become trapped in chaotic layers and preventing their accumulation in the midlayers. This outcome prevents the formation of dense middles layers and results in particles being dispersed over a wider area. If particles do form a midlayer layer, VSI becomes weakened, allowing the particles to accumulate in that layer, altering the VSI over time as particles move upward and the VSI slows, allowing the particles to settle further in the chaotic layer. This leads to a combination of areas with both a dense midlayer and particles trapped in the chaotic layer near the outer edge of the simulation. The disruption caused by VSI keeps particles from settling further in the chaotic layers, maintaining a horizontal distribution of particles. If the VSI becomes weakened, particles can settle below the 0.5 scale height threshold, but will never become concentrated in the midlayers, remaining scattered above this threshold. This research suggests that even if particles do accumulate in protoplanetary disks, VSI will continuously redistribute them, preventing the formation of midlayers and maintaining a horizontal distribution of solids. This outcome is consistent with exo-ejecta observations seen in some young star disks. The simulation results also reveal a specific scale of disks (10 to 100 AU in radius) suitable for VSI, demonstrating how VSI declines in larger disks (greater than 100 AU in radius) due of their stable inner regions. In these larger disks, outer regions may still exhibit VSI, contributing to the dispersal of particles and reducing the risk of midlayer formation, also supporting exo-ejecta observations. Recently introduced dynamic entrance networks have been shown to be effective in addressing sample size imbalance, by allocating different amounts of weight to individual data points on a case-by-case basis. However, the current fixed representation of data points, which are combined using an additive method, can be optimized for further performance improvement. In this work, we modify the dynamic entrance network to use global mean pooling, which leads to a drop in average scores for adversarial attacks. Our proposed approach, which uses global mean pooling in dynamic entrance networks, achieves higher classification accuracy compared to the existing method, while demonstrating robustness in presence of data imbalance. We validate our findings through comprehensive experiments conducted on six datasets. In particular, our method yields outstanding performance when compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches, including baseline methods with different data imbalance scenarios, as well as enriched adversarial training. We also open-source our code and the associated model.

To effectively address open-domain commonsense question answering, it's essential to explore methods that analyze the connection between questions and available web documents. Current approaches primarily focus on incorporating rich representations, without sufficient attention to the semantic connections between questions and relevant documents. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel approach, constructing a set of question-document pairs with varying levels of semantic connection. These pairs, ranked along a connection spectrum from coarse to precise, serve as the core training data for a semi-supervised learning strategy. In response to an incoming question, our model generates a set of question-document pairs with diverse connection levels, and we select the most relevant document to provide the final answer. To avoid explicit relationship modeling, our approach leverages the intrinsic value of question documents ranked by similarity, thereby avoiding the risk of amplified noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods along with intriguing insights into the optimal connection level for answering open-domain commonsense questions. The code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Coarse-to-Precise.

A systematic review is conducted to investigate the presence of knowledge gaps in previously studied spectral properties of molecular cations containing oxygen. Specifically, theoretical spectra for 37 cometary molecules, which exist or are plausible and have been studied in cationic form, are systematically calculated using multiple methods and across a range of solar wavelengths. However, it is found that only 7 of these molecules have associated composite spectra available in the current database, leaving a vast amount of computational data in need of integration. Mental wellness within the criminal justice system has long been a pressing concern.  To address this challenge, many jurisdictions are considering the effectiveness of mandatory mental health treatments for offenders.  This study examines data on Ontario, Canada's offenders undergoing court-ordered treatment and mental health assessments between 2004 and 2014.  A difference-in-differences approach is employed to assess the impact of mandatory mental health treatments on offenders' mental wellness, relying on data from the Ontario Mental Health Standards instrument.  The research reveals that court-ordered mental health treatments lead to modest improvements in offenders' overall mental wellness, with the positive outcomes being more pronounced in jail-based programs.  Furthermore, the analysis shows that such programs result in a significant reduction in recidivism among offenders with low levels of education, and that jail-based programs lead to greater reductions in violent recidivism among this subgroup.  The findings also indicate that sentencing court-based programs in jail or in the community makes a significant difference, with community-based programs showing greater effectiveness in promoting offenders' mental wellness and reducing violent and property-related offenders in the justice system.  The study highlights the effectiveness of court-ordered mental health treatments and community-based programs in particular, and suggests that these programs could be further enhanced by providing educational support to offenders with low levels of education.  The research was conducted in collaboration with the Ontario government and various justice and mental health stakeholders, and the findings are relevant to other jurisdictions that are considering the effectiveness of similar programs.  The study's results can be verified by other academics, and the data used in the research is publicly available, allowing for Replication of the research.  The findings of the research have significant implications for policy makers, suggesting that investing in mental health treatments and community-based programs could result in substantial cost savings for the justice system and social welfare system, and could also boost offenders' mental wellness, reduce their offending rates, and boost their employment opportunities.  The research also highlights the importance of taking into account the different needs of offenders with different levels of education in designing and implementing effective mental health treatments and community-based programs. Quantum systems' behavior can be highly unpredictable due to their sensitive response to initial conditions, as demonstrated in the seminal work of von Neumann and Wigner. To further understand the instability and complexity of these systems, chaos theory provides a valuable framework. In this study, we apply graph neural networks to analyze the instability of a quantum system, specifically the Heisenberg lattice model, relying on a custom architecture that generates a vector representing the system's instability. This setup allows for comparison of unstable vectors through a cosine similarity metric, yielding insights into how instability propagates and connects local actions to global effects. By interpreting the learned variables using our architecture, we identify key aspects of instability, including periodic dynamics, node-specific chaos, and the impact of connection variety on system instability. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our framework provides precise information to compare local units' instability, offering a solution to the challenge of determining the complexity of a system's dynamics. In the Heisenberg lattice model analysis, we observe that the application of context-dependent connections reduces chaos, revealing a crucial interunit relationship that contributes to the system's unstable behavior. This work introduces a novel graph neural network-based method for analyzing the instability of a system, with the Heisenberg lattice model serving as a specific example. This framework's explainable characteristics allow us to gain a deeper understanding of chaos, demonstrating the complexity of its dynamics through unit-specific variables and providing a similarity-based metric for comparing the context-dependent units' instability. In the process, we discover a crucial aspect of the Heisenberg lattice model's unstable behavior that has not been previously reported. The code and the paper's figures are available at https://github.com/ghulam-saeed/Graph-Based-Chaos-Detection. The results are a superset of those presented in Quantum Information Processing, 2022. Consider a parametric model based on independent observations from one of several possible distributions, where the underlying distribution is unknown and the parameters of the model are treated as mixed across a known range. We aim to estimate the average of the model's parameters using maximum likelihood estimation methods. We examine two specific cases: one where the distribution of the model's parameters follows a normal distribution and another where the distribution is unknown. In both instances, we establish that the average of the model's parameters can be estimated by taking the sample average of the observed data. This finding holds under regularity conditions and holds specifically without condition where the distribution of the model's parameters is discrete. We also explore scenarios where the range of the mixture distribution changes over time and is unknown, and provide examples from exponential and Weibull distributions. Furthermore, we discuss the consistency of various estimators of the model's parameters, and provide a generalized empirical likelihood estimator of the model's parameters. We conclude by examining a simulation where the distribution of the model's parameters changes over time and is unknown, and where the range of the mixture distribution is known. We also analyze real data from (i) an experiment where the response variable was measured over time, and where the distribution of the model's parameters was unknown and changed over time, and (ii) a study on the strength of concrete beams submitted to free freeze-thaw cycles, where the distribution of the model's parameters was mixed and unknown. We further analyze a simulation and a real data set from the field of ecology. We end by discussing some open problems in this area. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint H I mass galaxy, is anomalous in its lack of both recent star formation and an active galactic nucleus. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among trajectory data, resulting from diverse degree of success in achieving the desired goal. In response to this challenge, we develop a novel method called Positive Trajectory Learning in offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement learning (PTL-MARL). This approach identifies high-successful trajectory data and prioritizes their utilization for learning. By focusing on effective data, our method eliminates the negative impact of less successful experiences and expands the range of successful behaviors by targeting the distribution of successful experiences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by incorporating multiple distinct methods of interacting with environment and multiple degree of success distributions, yielding performance gains over existing methods. Our work is valued for its simple design, scalable nature, and substantial performance enhancements, paving the way for improved offline learning among complex interactions. Our code is available at github.com/vahidh/Learning-From-Positive-Trajectories.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 13 actions per second, largely because of strict safety checks required to prevent agents from exploiting exploited exploits.
Our work introduces TextWorldExpress, a high-speed text-based game framework that accelerates safety-aware text-based games to an incredible one million actions per second on a single GPU, without sacrificing fundamental challenge and consistency with real-world games. 
TextWorldExpress boasts three distinct evaluation protocols to demonstrate its capabilities, showcasing the framework's potential to enhance current methods of assessing agents rapidly, as well as its suitability for training more-effective virtual teaching tools. 
One such tool, TextWorldExpress has enabled a 50-fold acceleration in training current state-of-the-art models, setting a new benchmark in text-based games. 
Our findings are available in the paper TextWorldExpress: Imitating Text Games at One Million Steps Per Second.

We introduced a novel mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous medium, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures could be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. There are two distinct fracture categories: (1) perfectly conducting fractures, which have no resistance and allow seamless fluid flow, and (2) critically conducting fractures, whose flow resistance is negligible due to high fracture conductivity. Our model features a hybrid mixed approach for capturing flow patterns within both types of fractures. This method involves utilizing continuous potential functions, along with discrete velocity fields, limited to the centroids of specific elements, particularly within the matrix component. Differential operators, including a divergence, are applied to determine the velocity fields within these elements, whereas the norm of these fields is determined through a norm associated with the space of fractures. This method also employs a hybrid version of the underlying problem, involving the application of both the balance equation and the compatibility condition in fractures, along with consistent numerical schemes. Our previous work demonstrated the consistency and stability of this method, along with convergence properties. Furthermore, this method yields significant computational advantages, given the significantly reduced number of unknowns compared to traditional mixed finite element methods. This is particularly evident in three-dimensional scenarios. Our numerical experiments, conducted on various test cases, demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in approximating solutions, along with the significant computational benefits of using only linear solvers to obtain the discrete velocity and potential fields. This is a distinct improvement over the typical mixed finite element approach, which involves more intricate and slower solvers, particularly for complex and high-resolution scenarios. This method can be applied to various real-world scenarios, including but not limited to, geological domains, annotated tissue, and porous cement pastes, along with other fractured porous media. This paper presents the results of these numerical experiments, in addition to a detailed explanation of the underlying theory. This includes a brief review of the relevant existing literature, along with a hybrid mixed formulation of the underlying problem, along with the derivation of the associated a posteriori error bounds. Mobile agents require accurate navigation, and VIO techniques can provide this by combining visual and inertial data. However, these systems typically use recurrent models to process inertial observations, which can result in performance degradation over extended periods. This issue arises because the state is limited to the size of the hidden state in traditional RNNs, which can't effectively capture the correlation between inertial signals and the navigation state over time. In response to this challenge, we introduce an external memory attention model in VIO, which we call EMA-VIO, to handle navigation by paying attention to certain inertial observations that are relevant to the current state. This approach allows our model to efficiently process inertial data even in prolonged scenarios. We also introduce a new orientation estimation method to enhance the robustness of orientation estimation. In our experiments, EMA-VIO demonstrated superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art VIO systems, with our system showing a 25% reduction in the rotation estimation error and a 30% reduction in the translation estimation error in the office and hotel scenarios. Moreover, we found a significant improvement in estimation accuracy when applying orientaion regularization and external memory attention in both scenarios. Notably, our system outperformed existing VIO systems even when comparing translation estimation error rates, which we believe is a novel finding. We also successfully integrated a lidar sensor with EMA-VIO and observed a relatively small boost in estimation accuracy in comparison to the inertial-only setting. Our system's efficiency and effectiveness are demonstrated by a 5 times reduction in translation estimation error when comparing the floor plan navigation task with the inertial-only setting. In conclusion, our system's innovative external memory attention mechanism makes it an advanced method for deep VIO, and our orientation estimation technique enhances the robustness of orientation estimation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ShangYueXu/EMA-VIO.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye lenses, we propose a novel concept where multiple lobster-eye lenses are combined to cover a common field of view. Each lens is attached to a separate image sensor, and the arrangement of the system is designed such that the optical path is completely isolated between the lenses and their adjacent sensors. This concept could potentially decrease the total cost of such monitors by minimizing the number of image sensors needed. Furthermore, this design facilitates easier replacement of the lenses and allows for the use of more sophisticated image sensors. We demonstrate the optical functionality of this multi-lens design through simulations and physical experiments, and explore various applications for this concept in the context of present and future X-ray telescopes. The scale at which this concept can be implemented makes it an interesting option for future large-aperture X-ray telescopes, including those with telescopes consisting of many small mirrors. The proposed design can be implemented in various ways to optimize the performance of the system, and multiple feasible configurations have been identified. The proposed multi-lens design can also be used in conjunction with different optical elements, such as curved image sensors, and has the potential to be used in other fields of science beyond X-ray astronomy. The ease with which the image sensors and lenses can be swapped out in this design provides opportunities for implementing various novel optical techniques, such as artificial intelligence, in the analysis of the data. The proposed concept can be implemented in a range of scales, from a few centimeters to many meters in length, which makes it suitable for a wide range of applications, from desktop experimental setups to large telescopes with a massive aperture. The performance of the proposed multi-lens design has been assessed in a range of simulations, and a range of possible configurations for this design have been identified in the context of X-ray astronomy. The proposed multi-lens design provides an optical system with a wide field of view and a high spatial resolution, which makes it a highly effective and powerful tool for a wide range of applications in the field of X-ray astronomy. Despite the significant progress in document extraction techniques, a major obstacle in their widespread use is the time-consuming and costly process of labeling documents. In this work, we demonstrate that labeling just 500 images is sufficient to achieve high accuracy in extracting information from visually complex documents, a common challenge in many countries where documents are widely used. To achieve this, we employed a novel approach to sample documents for training and validation, relying on a broadly applicable dataset with rich visual content, specifically financial transaction documents. Our findings were consistently shown across multiple evaluation metrics and two different model types. To further validate our findings, we collected a new dataset with 20,000 labeled entries, achieving an F1 score of 87% with 500 labeled samples. Our results have significant implications for implementing document extraction at a large scale, making it more feasible with a much smaller team of labelers. Our code and datasets are available for public use.

For autonomous navigation, especially in complex and dynamic indoor environments, selecting the optimal path involves weighing factors like obstacle avoidance, representation accuracy, and operational efficiency. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that employs a simple layered framework for sonar sensor output, combining signals to create a more precise representation for path planning. The proposed method filters out sonar signals to eliminate unnecessary readings, reducing data quantity and speeding up navigation computations. The selected sonar signals are then categorized into three layers, each dealing with a particular distance range that is processed differently. The middle layer, with the most significant impact on navigation, is particularly important as it combines sonar readings to enhance accuracy and accuracy-based decision making in the n-layer navigation framework. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through navigation tests in a real world setting using the iAMRRT algorithm. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In this research, we introduce HiTMap, a novel graph-based representation to determine optimal paths in unknown environments. This model divides a map into overlapping rectangular sections, assigning each a distinct signature based on the features within. When two sections overlap, their signatures combine in a way that reflects the map's actual structure. To determine the best path, HiTMap uses a comparison function to combine the signature of the robot's current position with those of potential next locations. Our experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show that HiTMap outperforms existing methods in terms of mapping size, navigation efficiency, and robustness. Moreover, HiTMap's flexibility allows it to be integrated with other mapping techniques, such as SLAM, by using the same comparison function to determine the areas to be incorporated into the map. Our research also explores the relationship between the efficiency of HiTMap and various map parameters, paving the way for further optimizations. HiTMap's code is available at https://github.com/Pranav-TT/HiTMap.

This research explores a type of statistical model called finite mixture models, which is used to analyze and interpret complex data. We show that these models can be connected to two related fields: geometric probability and Choquet theory. In the process, we define a specific parameter called the mixture model's centroid, which has interesting properties. For example, it remains unchanged when the data is rotated. We also discover that the centroid can be expressed as a weighted average of geometric shapes, which provides insight into its structure. This finding offers a statistical application of a mathematical concept called the convex combination of points within a geometric space, which can be extended to more complex shapes. This research is presented in collaboration with the team of Jean-Paul Doisy.

We present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator tailored for object-oriented programming on GPUs. By introducing a novel "allocation region" concept, DynaSOAr optimizes memory usage and reduces fragmentation. A concurrent approach is taken to allocate memory, both globally and locally, to accommodate various use cases, including multi-threaded applications. A range of performance optimizations, including automatic detection and reduction of memory waste, improves memory efficiency further. A group G has an algebraic diameter of n if its largest subgroup with an n-dimensional irreducible representation is nilpotent of order n. In this paper, we show that a finite group with an algebraic diameter of n has precisely n non-abelian simple module series, and these form a partition of the group's structure. Additionally, we find that groups with an algebraic diameter of n are rare, as they satisfy a certain condition related to the number of simple module series and the algebraic diameter n. Specifically, this condition is defined as the absence of a specific pattern in the group's structure, which can be conceptualized as solvability in a particular dimension. In fact, this condition is equivalent to solvability in (n-1) dimensions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for n greater than 4, there are no finite groups that satisfy this condition, thus implying that groups with an algebraic diameter of n greater than 4 are non-existent. However, for n equal to 4, we provide an example of an existing finite group, which is the symmetric group S4, proven by Bertrand. On the other hand, we offer an alternative, more concise proof of this fact. Lastly, we offer a solution to the original problem posed by Bertrand.

As processor cores, memory and RAM are now part of every smartphone, a significant source of heat is generated within the device itself. Accurate thermal management relies on knowing the internal temperature, making it necessary to design a temperature detection system that can be integrated into these devices. This paper presents a novel digital temperature detection algorithm that uses only a single bit of thermal resistance information and a known supply voltage. This leads to a highly efficient and small temperature detection system with only a single bit of thermal resistance information required, achieving a temperature accuracy of 1.5°C in a 90nm CMOS process. A working example based on this algorithm was implemented in a 65nm CMOS process with a 1.8V supply voltage, and successfully detected temperatures between 0.6V to 1.8V. A comprehensive analysis of various system error sources including thermal resistance, supply voltage, bit resolution and conversion period on the temperature detection accuracy is also presented. A working temperature detection chip was designed with a 10bit ADC and a thermal controller, achieving a temperature resolution of 0.24°C, a maximum error of 1.4°C, a small footprint of 0.04mm^2, and a low power consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion, also supporting both external and internal thermal resistance modes. A comparison with existing temperature detection chips including Texas Instruments's TMS370 and Analog Devices's AD7415 shows this design has a higher resolution, a smaller footprint and a lower power consumption. A temperature gradient detection function was also designed and tested, and possible applications of this design in wireless sensor nodes, wearable devices and automotive systems also discussed. They also determined the direction of the nebula's expanding shell and calculated its age. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by a rough surface's texture, which can be hazardous for safety in various contexts such as waterways, surface skidding, and gas and oil extraction. To address this issue, research focuses on identifying effective texture patterns to minimize friction and associated problems. Previously, studies have demonstrated that anisotropic crystal formations in granular materials and two-dimensional cell patterns in liquid crystals exhibit optimal orientations that minimize friction. In contrast, this current study investigates the optimal texture patterns in liquid foams for minimizing friction. Due to the dynamic and highly unstable nature of foam crystals, direct measurement is challenging, thus we rely on theoretical approaches to analyze our findings. Specifically, we examined the geometry of foam crystals in two-scenario applications: surface textures and interface foams. In both cases, the orientation of the macroscopic crystal pattern influences the flow resistance significantly. Furthermore, we determine the most resistant and stable orientations of these patterns, which can be critical in preventing unsafe surface flow and improving the efficiency of gas and oil extraction. Moreover, our research reveals that circular ring textures exhibit high resistance compared to other patterns, which could be an interesting feature in its own right. Overall, our study on texture-induced friction in liquid foams highlights potential solutions for various industrial and everyday contexts. Lastly, we believe that this research can be extended to other complex non-Newtonian liquids beyond liquid foams.

The sole monitoring and removal of cancerous skin growths is not sufficient, as there's also the risk of treating benign lesions, which can happen with many carcinomas. To reduce the number of such instances, doctors recommend a more precise diagnosis based on biopsy results. We propose an approach to improve the accuracy of dermatologists' initial assessments by analyzing images of skin lesions. We use a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNN) and statistical techniques to assess both the image classification confidence and features for anomalies, which are then used to estimate the risk of carcinomas in each image category. To test our method, we used two datasets: PH**2 and SKI-89 containing 479 and 248 images respectively. We found that our proposed method is particularly effective in identifying outlier samples and can be a valuable tool for dermatologists in clinical environments. With simple hardware, our implementation can analyze a new skin biopsy in approximately 1 second, and our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abdi-rahman/derma-carcinoma-risk-assessment. We believe this approach has potential applications in other screening and detection tasks that involve the presence of outlier samples. Moreover, to validate our method, we conducted additional experiments using a dataset with malignant and benign skin lesion classifications, and found that our approach is effective in identifying carcinomas, with a moderate gain in accuracy of 6% compared to a leading baseline, and can be further improved with the inclusion of additional features, to provide a more comprehensive risk assessment protocol. To enhance the practical utility of our method, we created a web application that allows easy access to the code and demonstrates the risk assessment process for a sample dataset. Contrary to expectations, our observations reveal that increasing the rate of wall rotation leads to a transition from a stable, constant-speed interface to instability and the development of curved fingers. When the interface is straight, a known result shows that increasing rotation accelerates the interface speed. This occurs when the interface forms a semi-circle or we observe the development of fingering even in a cell with no initial defect. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that traditional attention mechanisms, when used for target word production, can be improved upon. We present a novel look-forward attention mechanism, designed to focus on the target words that have already been generated, in addition to the unproduced ones. We also introduce a new loss function, tailored to the test-time process of predicting the next word. We demonstrate that both the look-forward attention and additional loss function are crucial components, with the former outperforming traditional mechanisms and the latter gaining significance in its own right. We achieve state-of-the-art results on widely-used translation datasets, showcasing the efficacy of our method. Code is available at GitHub repository: https://github.com/ghrua/look-forward-attention.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus segmentation in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus primarily on image reconstruction, the proposed network places a superior point annotation value as the supervised task, resulting in a better annotation, as demonstrated by various evaluation metrics. Moreover, the model's versatility is highlighted by its applicability to various W-shaped architectures, making it suitable for a wide range of medical image annotation applications. The code for this research has been made available at GitHub: https://github.com/zwang84/W-Net. The proposed model's performance was also tested in a ranking task, which yielded a 6.15% relative accuracy improvement when evaluating on the CVC08 dataset, and a 13.85% relative accuracy improvement when evaluating on the CVC17 dataset. The proposed model has further applications in point-based organ segmentation, as illustrated by a case study on prostate gland segmentation, which yielded a 10.85% relative area distance improvement when evaluating on the CVC07 dataset. Building on this advancement, we introduced a Virtual Origin SA method to accurately determine lateral tissue displacement during scans. This new method generates precise data without the errors associated with mechanical scanner issues and environmental variations. Imaging technologies for human-computer interaction have the potential to link computer algorithms with human proofs and demonstrations, allowing for a more natural understanding and problem-solving. While success in this area would be significant, developing suitable methods to achieve it is challenging due to the variability and unclear underlying structures of human actions. In response to these difficulties, a new approach called "Rational Pseudocode" is proposed, which seeks to convert human demonstrations into readable pseudocodes while accounting for common ambiguities in imaging data. By representing demonstrations in this pseudocode format, their underlying logic and algorithms can be revealed and validated through normal mathematical means. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, it is applied to multiple types of algorithms, including those solved with pen and paper, and shows that in many cases, the structure of these algorithms remains accessible even after a decade. Furthermore, by examining the limitations and constraints of this method, it becomes apparent that certain algorithms cannot be derived from a single demonstration, requiring the use of multiple demonstrations to solve them. This issue is illustrated with the example of the famous Reidemeister move, for which multiple demonstrations are provided, and by analyzing its structure, it is shown that it corresponds to a specific type of algebra known as quasigroups, which is verified through direct comparison with an existing mathematical proof. This research also leads to a related problem of identifying the most minimal possible pseudocodes that can represent a given demonstration, which is shown to be equivalent to the problem of determining the minimal number of axes required to define an overlying structure, and can be solved using a simple algorithm. This approach and associated challenges are further explored through the example of the Baxter pipe dream, which is a celebrated mathematical object with an unclear and unsolved definition, and for which the method of rational pseudocode reveals a possible connection to the theory of clustered quasigroups. This research also results in a usable software tool available online for downloading. This work is an invitation to mathematicians and computer scientists to collaborate and provide guidance in order to further develop the method of rational pseudocode in order to solve the challenging problem of defining the Baxter pipe dream. This paper was originally published in the Proceedings of the 2021 ACM Conference on Human Information Interaction and Retrieval, Honolulu, HI, USA, March 2021.

We find that at high levels of competition, evasion groups often form large, sparse divisions, potentially leading to catastrophic outcomes for individual agents within the same group. benefit multiple-learning tasks by preventing the loss of information and
enhancing the overall performance. However, when tasks are mutually exclusive, a
common representation can also suffer from competing interests, leading to
slow learning and decreased performance. This negative effect gets even more
intensified in temporal multi-task reinforcement learning settings, where it causes
performance fluctuations and further slows down learning. To address this
issue-related context, we propose a modular module-based method of approximately
separating tasks and representing shared information in isolated systems. By
doing so, it prevents the interference that occurs with a shared representation and
allows for better performance in temporal multi-task reinforcement learning. We
test this method on simple examples and more complex games like the human-made
mini games of the Atari 2600 suite and the complexly designed single-player
game of SPL, and our findings show that our method yields superior performance
in both cases. We also explore different levels of system isolation and find
that an appropriate level of modulation is crucial for achieving the best
results. Additionally, we discover that our method effectively prevents the
destructive interference that causes low performance in challenging contexts like
the game of SPL. Finally, we conclude that our method provides a simple yet

Recently, machine learning techniques have encountered challenges related to data inverses, which stem from biased data and compromise the fairness criterion. This research focuses on an important yet difficult problem: extracting data from one class's posterior probabilities. A novel approach is proposed, leveraging conditional GANs and an L2 regularization method to enhance performance. Experiments with both biased binary classification and multi-classified data demonstrate the benefits of this innovative technique. Compared to current solutions and GAN-based counterparts, our proposed method achieves superior results, as validated by multiple assessment metrics. The code associated with this research can be accessed at https://github.com/lingeshm/regularized_CGAN_Fairness.

This article examines the possibility of finding invariant surfaces in dynamical systems governed by fractional-order differential equations. To accomplish this aim, we divide the differential equation into two parts: one part consisting of whole order differential equations and the other part consisting of fractional-order differential equations with a specific derivative order. We then determine the requirements for these two parts to accommodate invariant surfaces. Specifically, we find that the whole order part must be nondegenerate and have at least three dimensions, whereas the fractional-order part requires a specific derivative order of two with certain symmetry conditions. We also establish that any surface that is invariant under these systems can be defined by a specific equation involving the derivative operator. Finally, we outline the necessary procedures to determine the invariance of a surface, including the application of the derivative operator to determine and verify the derivative order, and the use of the surface's equation to determine the system's dimensions and determine whether they satisfy the required conditions. We then provide an example of a system with an invariant surface to illustrate these concepts. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between invariant surfaces and compact manifolds, and provide an example of a system with a surface that is not invariant to demonstrate the importance of the differential order in this context. Lastly, we outline the necessary procedures to extend the possibility of finding invariant surfaces to systems defined by partial differential equations and fractional-order differential equations in higher dimensions.
